topics.title: Forecasting risk and what-if analysis
topics.summary: Every NPV rests on forecasts, and forecasts can be wrong. This topic gives you four tools for seeing how much a forecasting error could hurt: sensitivity analysis (one input at a time), scenario analysis (several inputs together), simulation (random inputs, look at the whole output distribution) and NPV break-even (how far an input can move before NPV hits zero).

topics.title: Break-even points and operating leverage
topics.summary: Break-even asks how many units we must sell. Cash break-even covers cash costs, accounting break-even also covers depreciation, and financial break-even also earns the required return (NPV = 0), so they always come in that order. Operating leverage then shows how strongly operating cash flow reacts to a change in sales volume.

topics.title: Real options
topics.summary: A real option is the right, but not the obligation, to expand, abandon, wait or change production later, once we know more. Flexibility has value, so ignoring it understates NPV. Decision trees, working from right to left with probabilities and NPVs that are already discounted, put a number on that value.

concepts.definition: The risk that we make a bad investment decision because the projected cash flows are wrong, for example accepting a project that only looks like positive NPV because the forecasts were too optimistic.
concepts.explain: Every NPV rests on forecasts of sales, price, costs and project life, and each forecast can be wrong. The danger is greatest for a new product with no history. The first line of defence is to ask what specific source of value makes the NPV positive; the what-if tools of this chapter then show how much damage an error would do.
concepts.example: Prairie Paws Pet Foods computes NPV = +$420,000 for a new dog biscuit from a survey-based sales forecast. If real sales come in far below the survey the true NPV is negative, even though the arithmetic was perfect: the forecast, not the formula, was wrong.
concepts.contrast: Forecasting risk is the danger (inputs that may be wrong); sensitivity, scenario, simulation and NPV break-even are the tools that measure it. It is not the market risk (σ, β) of Chapters 12-13 and not a spreadsheet typo.
concepts.trap: A positive NPV does not prove value creation. Positive-NPV projects are rare in competitive markets, so a large NPV with no stated source of value is a warning sign. Cue words: new product, optimistic forecast, rivals will respond.
concepts.mnemonic: Garbage in, garbage out: NPV is only as good as the forecast.

concepts.definition: Change one input at a time, hold every other input at its base-case value, recompute the NPV and measure ΔNPV/Δinput. With N inputs this takes 2N + 1 full DCF runs: one base case plus one up-run and one down-run per input.
concepts.explain: It shows which single forecast NPV is most sensitive to, so we know where forecasting errors do the most damage. A steep ΔNPV/Δinput means a small error moves NPV a lot. NPV is a straight line in price, quantity and unit costs, so the slope is the same whichever second value you test. It points to the problem but gives no accept or reject rule.
concepts.contrast: Sensitivity flexes ONE input over a broad range (2N + 1 runs); scenario flexes SEVERAL inputs together (3 runs for base, best, worst); simulation draws all inputs at random; NPV break-even solves for the input value where NPV = 0.
concepts.trap: ΔNPV needs the annuity factor (multiply the ΔOCF by it); price, quantity and cost changes are taxed, so use (1 − T), but the CCA shield T·D does not change. Compare inputs on the same percentage change, because a per-unit slope depends on the units.
concepts.formula: ΔNPV/Δx = (NPV_new − NPV_base)/(x_new − x_base); number of runs = 2N + 1

concepts.definition: Change several inputs together, in a sensible and consistent way, to build a few cases (typically base, best and worst) and compute the NPV of each. The results are not linear in the input changes because fixed costs do not scale with volume.
concepts.explain: Best case: price and quantity up, variable and fixed costs down. Worst case: the reverse. It shows what can happen and how bad the downside is, but not how likely each case is: to get an expected NPV you must add probabilities (E[NPV] = Σ p × NPV). More and more scenarios only add possibilities, not a decision rule.
concepts.example: Okotoks Trailer Works (outlay $900,000, 4 years, D = $225,000, T = 30%, R = 12%): base P = $2,400, v = $1,350, Q = 1,200, FC = $620,000 gives NPV = $665,753.59. Worst case (P and Q −10%, v and FC +10%): OCF = $100,400.00, NPV = −$595,050.13. Best case (P and Q +10%, v and FC −10%): NPV = $2,117,910.31.
concepts.contrast: Scenario = a few hand-picked consistent combinations; sensitivity = one input at a time; simulation = thousands of random combinations. Scenarios give a handful of NPVs, simulation gives a distribution.
concepts.trap: Best case means EVERY input moves the favourable way, so costs go DOWN; moving a cost the wrong way is the classic slip. A 10% favourable move in every input does not change NPV by 10%. Probabilities must sum to 1 before you weight the NPVs.
concepts.mnemonic: Best = revenues up, costs down. Worst = the reverse.
concepts.formula: E[NPV] = Σ p_s × NPV_s (Σ p_s = 1); OCF = [(P − v)Q − FC](1 − T) + T·D

concepts.definition: Let a computer draw every uncertain input at random from a chosen probability distribution, compute the NPV for each draw, repeat thousands of times and study the distribution of NPV (mean, spread, chance of NPV < 0), not only its expected value.
concepts.explain: It combines scenario analysis (all inputs change) with sensitivity analysis (each input takes many values). The shape of the output matters: it will probably not be symmetrical and the baseline or expected value may not sit at the peak. It needs a distribution for every input and a view on how inputs move together, and it gives no simple decision rule.
concepts.example: A rail terminal has eight uncertain inputs. The analyst assigns a distribution to each, runs 10,000 trials and finds a mean NPV of +$310,000 but a negative NPV in 35% of the trials. The mean alone would have hidden that chance of loss.
concepts.contrast: Simulation is not scenario analysis (a few hand-picked cases) and not sensitivity analysis (one input at a time). Unlike NPV break-even it does not solve for a threshold: it describes the whole range of outcomes.
concepts.trap: Do not answer "the average NPV" when the question asks about risk: the answer is the distribution. The simulated mean need not equal the base-case NPV. Independent draws can create unrealistic combinations if the inputs are related.

concepts.definition: The level of one input (price, quantity, EBITDA, variable cost) at which NPV = 0, all other inputs at base: how far the input can change before the decision to accept would change. It is the finance break-even, not the accounting (profit = 0) break-even.
concepts.explain: Write NPV = 0, replace the unknown input by a symbol and solve. Use an annuity factor for finite flows, a perpetuity for flows that never end, and include the CCA tax shield. Because EBITDA is pre-tax, the after-tax amount needed must be divided by (1 − T). At the break-even level IRR = R.
concepts.example: Lecture plant: cost $1,000,000, CCA straight-line over 8 years (simplified), income forever, R = 10%, T = 30%. DTS = 0.3 × 1,000,000 ÷ 8 = $37,500 a year, PV = 37,500 × 5.334926 = $200,059.73. NPV = −1,000,000 + 200,059.73 + (0.7 ÷ 0.10) × EBITDA = 0, so EBITDA = $114,277.18.
concepts.contrast: Sensitivity, scenario and simulation show how NPV moves; break-even asks where it hits zero. NPV (financial) break-even is higher than accounting break-even, because accounting profit ignores the required return.
concepts.trap: Gross the answer up for tax (÷(1 − T)), divide by an annuity factor and not by N, keep the CCA shield in the equation, and use a perpetuity when the income is perpetual. Giving the accounting (profit) break-even is wrong.
concepts.mnemonic: Set NPV = 0, solve for the one thing.
concepts.formula: NPV = 0 ⇒ EBITDA* = [I0 − PV(DTS)] ÷ [(1 − T) × annuity factor (or 1/R for a perpetuity)]

concepts.definition: The sales quantity at which operating cash flow is zero: Q_C = FC/(P − v). Depreciation is non-cash, so it is not part of the cash break-even.
concepts.explain: Each unit contributes P − v toward fixed cash costs. Below Q_C the project does not even cover its cash costs. At Q_C, OCF = 0, so the investment is never recovered: NPV = −I0, IRR = −100% and there is no payback. It is the lowest of the three break-evens.
concepts.example: P = $24, v = $15, FC = $90,000: contribution = $9 per unit, so Q_C = 90,000 ÷ 9 = 10,000 units.
concepts.contrast: Cash break-even leaves out depreciation; accounting break-even adds it (Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v)); financial break-even adds the required return. Order: Q_C < Q_A < Q_F.
concepts.trap: Do not add D to the cash break-even. The simple formula ignores tax; with taxes, setting OCF = 0 in Q = {FC + (OCF − T·D)/(1 − T)}/(P − v) can give a slightly lower figure because the CCA shield helps when income is negative.
concepts.mnemonic: Cash first: cover the cash costs.

concepts.definition: The sales quantity at which net income is zero: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v). At Q_A, OCF = D and no tax is paid, so the tax rate drops out of the formula.
concepts.explain: Each unit must cover variable cost, fixed cost and depreciation. Because profit is zero there, tax is zero, and Q_A is the same with or without taxes. At Q_A the project just recovers its investment over its life: IRR = 0%, payback = N years and NPV = I0[(1/N) × annuity factor − 1], which is negative.
concepts.example: Same project, with a $225,000 outlay depreciated over 5 years (D = $45,000): Q_A = (90,000 + 45,000) ÷ 9 = 15,000 units. At R = 10% the NPV at Q_A is 225,000 × (3.790787 ÷ 5 − 1) = −$54,414.60.
concepts.contrast: Accounting break-even makes profit zero (NI = 0); NPV or financial break-even makes NPV zero. Accounting is higher than cash (it adds D) and lower than financial (it ignores the required return).
concepts.trap: Forgetting D in the numerator, grossing up for tax (not needed at Q_A), or treating Q_A as the point where the project creates value. At Q_A, OCF = D, so (FC + OCF)/(P − v) gives the same number.

concepts.definition: The sales quantity at which NPV = 0: Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v), where OCF* = I0 ÷ annuity factor(R, N) is the constant OCF that just repays the investment at the required return. With taxes, Q_F = {FC + (OCF* − T·D)/(1 − T)}/(P − v). At Q_F, IRR = R.
concepts.explain: It is the break-even that matters to shareholders: a project can clear the cash and accounting break-evens and still sit below Q_F and lose value. First find OCF* from the annuity factor, then convert it to the quantity that produces it.
concepts.contrast: Q_C < Q_A < Q_F. OCF* uses the annuity factor (time value of money), whereas I0/N is the depreciation and leads back to the accounting break-even.
concepts.trap: Using I0/N instead of the annuity factor; forgetting the T·D and ÷(1 − T) steps when taxes are present; assuming that a project above the accounting break-even must have positive NPV.
concepts.formula: OCF* = I0 ÷ annuity factor(R, N); Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v); with taxes Q = {FC + (OCF* − T·D)/(1 − T)}/(P − v)

concepts.definition: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF = %ΔOCF ÷ %ΔQ: the percentage change in operating cash flow for a 1% change in quantity sold. At the accounting break-even, OCF = D, so DOL = 1 + FC/D.
concepts.explain: The more of the cost base is fixed, the more OCF swings when sales move, so high fixed costs mean high operating leverage and high forecasting risk. DOL is not constant: it falls as quantity rises (OCF grows) and rises as quantity falls.
concepts.contrast: DOL is a ratio of percentage changes, evaluated at one quantity; do not mix it up with the break-even quantities. Fixed costs are FC, without D, in the formula.
concepts.trap: Putting FC + D in the numerator, using the wrong OCF (it must be the OCF at the current quantity), or applying the old DOL after quantity has changed. The solutions manual derives a tax-adjusted form, but the course formula is the simple one.
concepts.mnemonic: More fixed cost per dollar of OCF, more leverage.
concepts.formula: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF; %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ; DOL at Q_A = 1 + FC/D

concepts.definition: An option is the right, but not the obligation, to do something in the future, decided later with information not available today. A financial option is a right to buy or sell a financial asset; a real option is a right to undertake a business initiative (expand, abandon, wait, change production). We usually pay a premium up front for it.
concepts.explain: We assume that when the decision time arrives we will make the best financial choice with the information then available. Because the right can be dropped when it is not worth using, an option never has negative value, so an NPV that ignores flexibility understates a project. Option pricing formulas are not examined here.
concepts.example: Building the freeway bridges longer than needed costs extra now (the premium) but keeps the right to widen the road cheaply later if traffic is heavy. Car insurance is the lecture's everyday example of a put option.
concepts.contrast: Option (right, free to walk away) vs obligation or forward (must act). Real option (business activity) vs financial option (security). Expansion, abandonment, timing and production flexibility are different kinds of real option.
concepts.trap: Don't treat the project as a now-or-never choice when the firm can adapt later. The premium is paid up front and must be compared with the value of the option. Match the example to the type: bigger machine or extra space = expansion; early exit = abandonment.
concepts.mnemonic: EATP: Expansion, Abandonment, Timing, Production flexibility.

concepts.definition: A diagram of today's choices, uncertain events with their probabilities and later decisions. Roll it back from right to left: at a decision node keep the best branch, at a chance node take the probability-weighted average E = Σ p × NPV, and at today's node compare the expected values including up-front costs.
concepts.explain: If the amounts on the tree are already NPVs (present values), no further discounting is needed. Choose at each later decision node before averaging at the earlier chance node, because we will pick the best action when we get there.
concepts.example: Freeway bridges (lecture numbers in $M, all already NPVs; busy road 80%, quiet 20%). Short bridges cost 120. If the road is busy, widening means knocking them down (20), building long bridges (160) and widening the surface (40) = 220, worse than the 150 cost to society of not widening, so we do not widen: 120 + 150 = 270; if quiet, 120. Expected cost = 0.8 × 270 + 0.2 × 120 = 240. Long bridges cost 160: if busy, widen for 40 (better than 150), total 200; if quiet, 160. Expected cost = 0.8 × 200 + 0.2 × 160 = 192. Build long bridges (192 < 240): the 40 premium saves 150 − 40 = 110 in the busy state, worth 0.8 × 110 = 88.
concepts.contrast: Decision node (we choose, take the best branch) vs chance node (nature chooses, take the weighted average). A tree with NPVs on it is not discounted again.
concepts.trap: Averaging before deciding at a later node, forgetting to include the extra up-front cost of the flexible choice, discounting amounts that are already present values, or mixing costs (lower is better) with benefits (higher is better).
concepts.mnemonic: Roll back: decide at squares, average at circles.
concepts.formula: E = Σ p_i × NPV_i (chance node); value of a decision node = best branch

concepts.definition: The abandonment option is the right to shut down or sell a project's assets if it does badly: abandon when the abandonment (salvage or resale) value exceeds the PV of continuing. The expansion option is the right to scale up if it does well; its value is the probability of that outcome times the PV of the extra gain, discounted to today.
concepts.explain: Abandonment limits the losses, so ignoring it underestimates NPV. The abandonment value is also the opportunity cost of continuing. Expansion adds value only in the good state, so weight it by the probability of that state and discount it back.
concepts.example: A project's year-1 value is $9.0M if demand is high (50%) and only $1.5M if low (50%), but the assets can be sold for $2.4M. With the option: 0.5 × 9.0 + 0.5 × 2.4 = $5.70M; without: 0.5 × 9.0 + 0.5 × 1.5 = $5.25M. The option is worth $0.45M at year 1, or 0.45 ÷ 1.12 = $0.40M today at R = 12%.
concepts.contrast: Abandonment helps in the bad state (floor on value); expansion helps in the good state (upside). Both are real options, and both raise NPV above the static value.
concepts.trap: Compare the abandonment value with the PV of continuing at that date; do not average before deciding. Subtract the extra up-front cost of buying the flexibility, and discount an option value that arises in a later year.
concepts.mnemonic: Abandon when continuing is worth less than selling.
concepts.formula: Abandon if salvage > PV(continuing); option value = value with option − value without option; expansion value = p × gain ÷ (1 + R)

activities.title: Order the steps of a sensitivity analysis
activities.prompt: Put the steps of a sensitivity analysis in the correct order.
items: Compute the base-case NPV with every input at its expected value
Choose one input and change it, holding all other inputs at base values
Recompute the full DCF (OCF, then NPV) with the new input value
Repeat for every input and compare which slope is steepest
activities.explanation: Sensitivity analysis flexes one input at a time around the base case. The slope ΔNPV/Δinput is computed for each input in turn, and the steepest slope marks the forecast whose error does the most damage. With N inputs this is 2N + 1 runs.

activities.explanation: The lecture's four main types are expansion, abandonment, timing and production flexibility. The premium is paid up front for the right, and a real option concerns a business activity rather than a security.

activities.title: Match the break-even to its formula
activities.prompt: Match each term with its formula or meaning.
activities.explanation: Each break-even adds one layer: cash costs, then depreciation, then the required return. OCF* is the level of operating cash flow that repays the outlay at the required return, and DOL measures how strongly OCF reacts to a change in quantity.

activities.title: Roll back a decision tree
activities.prompt: Put the steps for solving a decision tree in the correct order.
items: Lay out today's choices, the uncertain events with their probabilities and the later decisions
Write the NPV (already discounted) at the end of every branch
Start at the far right and, at each later decision node, keep the better branch
At each chance node take the probability-weighted average of the values to its right
At today's decision node compare the expected values, including the up-front costs, and choose
activities.explanation: A tree is solved from right to left. We decide at the later nodes first (we will pick the best action when we get there) and only then average over the uncertain events. Averaging before deciding is the classic error.

formulas.name: Operating cash flow (tax shield form)
formulas.when: Recompute the yearly cash flow each time an input in a what-if analysis changes.
formulas.trap: The CCA shield T·D does not change when price, quantity or costs change; interest never appears.

formulas.name: Sensitivity of NPV to an input
formulas.when: Measure how much NPV moves per unit change in one input, all others at base.
formulas.trap: Use NPV, not OCF (multiply a ΔOCF by the annuity factor), and compare inputs on equal percentage changes.

formulas.name: Runs in a sensitivity analysis
formulas.when: Count the work for N uncertain inputs (base + up + down for each).
formulas.trap: A scenario analysis needs only one run per case (3 for base, best, worst), however many inputs there are.

formulas.name: Expected NPV across scenarios
formulas.when: Weight scenario or branch NPVs by their probabilities.
formulas.trap: Probabilities must sum to 1; a simple average is only right for equally likely cases.

formulas.name: Annuity factor
formulas.when: Value a level cash flow for N years, e.g. the DTS or the required OCF*.
formulas.trap: Use the project's N (not N − 1) and the same period for R.

formulas.name: Perpetuity
formulas.trap: After-tax income is (1 − T) × EBITDA; the perpetuity is not a growing one unless told.

formulas.name: NPV break-even (plant with DTS annuity and perpetual income)
formulas.formula: −I0 + DTS × AF(R, N) + (1 − T) × EBITDA ÷ R = 0, so EBITDA* = [I0 − DTS × AF(R, N)] × R ÷ (1 − T)
formulas.when: Find the pre-tax income that makes NPV exactly zero.
formulas.trap: Divide by (1 − T) to get pre-tax, and use the annuity factor for the shield, not 1/R.

formulas.name: PV of the CCA tax shield
formulas.when: Put the whole tax shield into one PV inside a break-even equation.
formulas.trap: Choose the right first-year factor (half-year rule: (1 + 0.5k)/(1 + k)) and discount the salvage term N years.

formulas.name: Cash break-even quantity
formulas.when: Sales level at which operating cash flow is zero.

formulas.name: Accounting break-even quantity
formulas.when: Sales level at which net income is zero.
formulas.trap: Tax drops out because profit is zero; at Q_A, OCF = D.

formulas.name: Financial break-even OCF
formulas.trap: I0/N is just the depreciation and leads back to the accounting break-even.

formulas.name: Financial break-even quantity
formulas.when: Sales level at which NPV = 0 (no taxes).

formulas.name: Break-even quantity with taxes
formulas.when: Quantity that produces a given OCF when the firm pays tax (OCF = OCF* for financial break-even).
formulas.trap: Convert the OCF target to a pre-tax amount: subtract T·D first, then divide by (1 − T).

formulas.name: NPV at the accounting break-even
formulas.when: Show that the accounting break-even loses value (IRR 0%, payback N years).

formulas.name: Degree of operating leverage
formulas.when: Measure how much OCF moves per 1% change in quantity.
formulas.trap: Use FC without D; DOL changes with Q.

formulas.name: OCF response to a change in quantity
formulas.when: Forecast the new OCF from a percentage change in sales.
formulas.trap: Compute the new DOL from the new OCF, not the old one.

formulas.name: DOL at the accounting break-even
formulas.when: Leverage at the point where net income is zero (OCF = D).

formulas.name: Abandonment rule and option value
formulas.formula: Abandon if salvage > PV(continuing); option value = value with option − value without option
formulas.when: Decide whether to shut a project down and value the flexibility.
formulas.trap: Compare at the decision date and discount the option value back to today.

formulas.name: Value of an expansion option
formulas.when: Value the right to expand when the good state has probability p.
formulas.trap: The gain arises only in the good state and lies in a later year, so discount it.

questions.stem: In project analysis, forecasting risk (also called estimation risk) is best described as:
options: the possibility of a bad decision because the projected cash flows contain errors
the variability of the project's returns relative to the market portfolio
the chance that the firm cannot raise enough capital to build the project
the risk that the arithmetic inside the NPV spreadsheet contains a typing mistake
questions.explanation: Forecasting risk is the danger that errors in the projected cash flows lead to the wrong accept or reject decision. It is about wrong inputs, not about market-wide return variability (that is the σ and β of Chapters 12-13) and not about spreadsheet typos.

questions.stem: Prairie Paws Pet Foods reports an NPV of +$420,000 for a new organic dog biscuit. The forecast rests on one customer survey in which shoppers said they would "definitely try" the product, and the main worry is that real sales will fall far short of the survey. This worry is best called:
options: liquidity risk
forecasting risk
interest-rate risk
the risk of an unsystematic event
questions.explanation: The worry is that projected cash flows (sales) are wrong and a poor decision follows: forecasting risk. Liquidity and interest-rate risk are about the firm's funding and rate exposure, not about the accuracy of the sales forecast.

questions.stem: Why is forecasting risk usually greatest for a brand-new product compared with replacing a worn-out machine?
options: new products are always taxed at a higher rate, which distorts the cash flows
replacement decisions have no cash flows to forecast, so the NPV rule cannot be applied
the NPV formula is only valid for products that already exist
there is no sales history, so unit sales and prices are much harder to predict
questions.explanation: A new product has no track record to anchor the sales and price forecasts, so the projected cash flows are likelier to be far off. A replacement still has cash flows, and the NPV formula applies to both.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a sensible response to forecasting risk?
options: ask what specific source of value makes the NPV positive
run sensitivity and scenario analyses to see which forecasts matter most
examine how well supported the sales forecast is before relying on it
assume that competitors will not react if the project turns out to be profitable
questions.explanation: Success attracts imitators, so assuming rivals will sit still builds optimism into the forecast and increases forecasting risk. The other three responses are exactly the defences the course recommends: find the source of value, run what-if analyses, and test the forecast.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates forecasting risk from the what-if techniques of this chapter?
options: forecasting risk is the danger of wrong inputs; sensitivity, scenario, simulation and NPV break-even measure how much damage such errors could do
forecasting risk is a technique that tells us which input to flex, and sensitivity analysis is the danger of wrong inputs
forecasting risk and scenario analysis are two names for the same thing
forecasting risk concerns cost estimates only, and the what-if techniques concern revenue estimates only
questions.explanation: Forecasting risk is the problem (inputs that may be wrong). The what-if techniques are the tools for seeing how sensitive NPV is to those inputs. They are not synonyms and they cover revenues and costs alike.

questions.stem: A project can show a positive NPV even though its true NPV is negative if the cash-flow forecasts were too optimistic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. NPV is only as good as the cash flows fed into it. Over-optimistic forecasts make a project look better than it is, which is exactly what forecasting risk means.

questions.stem: Once the NPV is calculated with the correct formula, forecasting risk has been eliminated.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A correct formula applied to wrong inputs still gives a wrong answer. Forecasting risk lives in the inputs, so it is managed with source-of-value questions and what-if analysis, not removed by arithmetic.

questions.stem: The possibility that errors in projected cash flows lead to a wrong accept or reject decision is called _____ risk.
options: systematic
liquidity
forecasting
default
questions.explanation: Forecasting risk (estimation risk) is the term for the danger that errors in projected cash flows cause a bad decision. Systematic risk is the market-wide part of a stock's risk (Chapter 13).

questions.stem: Great Plains Coffee Kiosks calculates NPV = +$150,000 for a kiosk in a mall that already has three established rivals. The analyst cannot name any cost, product or location advantage. What is the best response?
options: accept, because any NPV above zero creates value no matter how the forecast was reached
reject, because competition always drives the NPV of every project below zero
be suspicious: positive-NPV projects are rare when competition is stiff, so find the source of value first
raise the discount rate until the NPV falls to zero and treat the project as break-even
questions.explanation: Where competition is stiff, a positive NPV with no articulated edge should be viewed with suspicion. The course answer is to look for the source of value, not to accept blindly or to fudge the discount rate.

questions.stem: A what-if analysis shows that a new product's NPV stays positive even in the worst case the team defined. Which conclusion is the most reasonable?
options: forecasting risk looks lower for the ranges tested, but actual outcomes can fall outside the worst case
the project is risk-free, because its worst-case NPV is positive in the analysis
the base-case NPV must have been calculated incorrectly by the team
competitors can no longer affect the project's cash flows after launch
questions.explanation: A positive worst case is reassuring only for the ranges examined. The text warns that even worst-case scenarios may not be low enough, so forecasting risk is lower, not zero.

questions.stem: Why can success itself increase forecasting risk in a competitive market?
options: success lowers the required return, so earlier forecasts become invalid
success raises depreciation, which changes the cash flows
success raises the tax rate on the project's profits
success attracts imitators, who push volume and margins below the forecast
questions.explanation: If the project works, rivals will copy it and drive down volume and profit. A forecast that ignores that reaction is too optimistic, which is forecasting risk.

questions.stem: A retailer's expansion plan assumed each new store would serve 4,000 customers a week, but the stores actually serve 2,600 and two of them close. This episode illustrates:
options: capital rationing
forecasting risk
the multiple-IRR problem
reinvestment risk
questions.explanation: The plan failed because projected cash flows (traffic) were much higher than reality. That is forecasting risk. Rationing is about a budget limit and multiple IRRs are about sign changes, neither of which is described.

questions.stem: Projects X and Y both have a base-case NPV of $200,000. X's NPV turns negative if sales are 4% below forecast. Y's NPV stays positive until sales are 35% below forecast. Which statement is correct?
options: Y has the higher forecasting risk, because it can absorb a much larger shortfall in sales
X has the higher forecasting risk for sales; sensitivity or NPV break-even analysis exposes the difference
the two have the same forecasting risk, because their base-case NPVs are both $200,000
neither project has any forecasting risk, because both base-case NPVs are positive
questions.explanation: A small forecasting error flips X's decision, so X is far more exposed. Equal base NPVs hide this, which is why we flex the inputs instead of reading only the base case.

questions.stem: According to the text, the first line of defence against forecasting risk is to ask:
options: what IRR the project earns to one decimal place
how many decimal places the sales forecast should carry
what specific source of value makes this investment have a positive NPV
whether the project can be financed entirely with debt
questions.explanation: Before trusting a positive NPV, we should be able to point to something specific (a cost edge, a better product, a niche) that creates the value. Precision of the arithmetic or the financing mix does not address forecasting risk.

questions.stem: A team reports base-case NPV = +$55,000, worst-case NPV = −$310,000 and best-case NPV = +$190,000. Which reading is fairest?
options: accept, because a positive base-case NPV is all that matters for the decision
forecasting risk is significant: the downside exceeds the base-case gain, and the likelihood of each case matters
reject, because any negative scenario NPV means the project must fail and cannot be saved
average the three NPVs equally to −$21,666.67 and reject the project
questions.explanation: Scenario results show what can happen, not how likely it is. A base-case gain of $55,000 against a worst-case loss of $310,000 signals high forecasting risk. An equal-weight average is wrong unless the three cases are equally likely.

questions.stem: In a highly competitive market positive-NPV projects are common, so a large positive NPV needs no further explanation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Positive-NPV investments are probably not common, especially under stiff competition. If we cannot name a sound economic reason for expecting an edge, a large positive NPV should be viewed with suspicion because the forecast may be too optimistic.

questions.stem: Sensitivity analysis in project evaluation means:
options: changing several inputs together in a consistent best-case or worst-case story
changing one input at a time, holding the others at their base values, and seeing how NPV responds
letting a computer draw every input at random from a distribution
finding the input value at which accounting profit is exactly zero
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis flexes ONE input while every other input stays at its base-case value. Several inputs together is scenario analysis, random draws are simulation, and a zero crossing is a break-even analysis.

questions.stem: A sensitivity analysis on N inputs needs 2N + 1 full DCF calculations. The "+1" is:
options: the base case
the discount rate
the worst-case scenario
the summary table of results
questions.explanation: For each of the N inputs we run one version with the input up and one with it down (2N runs), plus one baseline run with every input at its base value.

questions.stem: Alder Creek Hotels recomputes the NPV of a renovation four times: occupancy 5% lower, occupancy 5% higher, nightly rate 5% lower and nightly rate 5% higher. Each time every other input stays at its base value. This technique is:
options: scenario analysis
simulation analysis
NPV break-even analysis
sensitivity analysis
questions.explanation: One input at a time with the rest held at base values is sensitivity analysis. Scenario analysis would move occupancy and rate together, and simulation would draw them randomly.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts sensitivity analysis with scenario analysis?
options: sensitivity analysis flexes several inputs together, while scenario analysis flexes one input at a time
sensitivity analysis flexes one input at a time (2N + 1 runs); scenario analysis flexes several together (often just three cases)
sensitivity analysis uses random draws, while scenario analysis does not
sensitivity analysis solves for the input that sets NPV to zero, while scenario analysis does not
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = one variable over a broad range, others frozen; scenario = all variables over a limited range, moved together in a sensible way. The distractors swap the definitions or borrow from simulation and break-even.

questions.stem: Why does a steep ΔNPV/Δinput slope signal high forecasting risk for that input?
options: a steep slope means the input is known with certainty, so errors cannot occur
a steep slope forces the project's IRR below zero in every scenario
a steep slope means the input affects only depreciation, not cash flow
a small error in that input produces a large change in NPV and could flip the decision
questions.explanation: Slope measures how much NPV moves per unit of input error. The steeper it is, the more damage a given forecasting mistake does, so that input deserves the most attention.

questions.stem: For the same 10% change, a project's NPV falls by $52,000 when unit sales are lower, by $18,000 when fixed costs are higher and by $96,000 when price is lower. Which conclusion follows?
options: NPV is most sensitive to price, so the price forecast deserves the most attention
fixed costs matter most because their NPV effect is the smallest
unit sales matter most because they are the first input listed
none of the forecasts matters because the NPV effects are all different
questions.explanation: With equal percentage changes, the largest NPV change marks the most sensitive input: price (−$96,000). The smallest effect belongs to fixed costs, which carry the least forecasting risk here.

questions.stem: Which statement about sensitivity analysis is NOT true?
options: it holds all other inputs at their base-case values
it shows where forecasting errors do the most damage
it tells management whether to accept the project
for an input that enters OCF linearly, the NPV-versus-input graph is a straight line
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis points to the inputs that matter but gives no accept or reject rule. The other statements are true; in particular, NPV is linear in price, quantity and unit costs.

questions.stem: A sensitivity analysis of a project with 5 uncertain inputs requires 11 full DCF calculations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. 2N + 1 = 2(5) + 1 = 11: one base case plus one up-run and one down-run for each of the 5 inputs.

questions.stem: Because NPV is a straight-line function of unit sales, ΔNPV/ΔQ comes out the same whichever second sales level is tested.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. NPV changes by a constant amount per unit, so any second sales level gives the same slope. The solutions manual notes that the choice of 70,000 units does not matter.

questions.stem: An analyst finds that NPV is far more sensitive to unit sales than to fixed costs. What is the most useful next step?
options: ignore unit sales, because they are too uncertain to forecast
drop fixed costs from the model and recompute the NPV
spend effort, such as market research, to firm up the unit-sales forecast
replace the NPV rule with the payback rule for this project
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis tells us where errors do the most damage; the sensible response is to improve the forecast of the sensitive input.

questions.stem: In a sensitivity analysis, what comes immediately after computing the base-case NPV?
options: change every input to its worst value together at once
draw all inputs at random thousands of times from distributions
change one input, hold the rest at base values, and recompute the NPV
solve for the input at which NPV equals zero exactly
questions.explanation: The sequence is: base-case NPV, flex one input and recompute, form ΔNPV/Δinput, repeat for each input, compare. Moving everything together is a scenario, and random draws are simulation.

questions.stem: Boreal Coffee Roasters is evaluating a $360,000 roasting line for a 6-year project with no salvage. Base case: price $14.00 per bag, variable cost $8.50 per bag, 52,000 bags per year, fixed costs $140,000 per year. The CCA tax shield is treated as straight-line, so D = $60,000 per year. T = 30% and the required return is 11% per annum. Using a second price of $15.00, find the sensitivity of NPV to price, ΔNPV/ΔP, in dollars of NPV per $1 change in price.

errors.label: Ignored the (1 − T) factor
errors.explain: A dollar of extra price is taxed: only (1 − T) of it reaches OCF. The slope is Q(1 − T) × annuity factor, not Q × annuity factor.

errors.label: Reported ΔOCF/ΔP and never applied the annuity factor
errors.explain: $36,400 is the change in each year's OCF. NPV moves by that amount in every one of the 6 years, so multiply by the annuity factor.

errors.label: Used a 5-year annuity factor
errors.explain: The project lasts 6 years, so the annuity factor must use N = 6.

questions.explanation: Raising price by $1 adds Q(1 − T) = 52,000 × 0.7 = $36,400 to OCF in each of the 6 years. Discounted at 11%, that is $36,400 × 4.230538 ≈ $153,991 of NPV per $1 of price. Rerunning the full DCF at two prices and dividing gives the same slope.

questions.stem: In the Boreal Coffee Roasters project the price is $14.00 and the variable cost is $8.50 per bag, fixed costs are $140,000 per year, the life is 6 years, T = 30% and the required return is 11% per annum. By how much does NPV fall if unit sales come in 6,000 bags below the 52,000-bag forecast?

steps.label: ΔOCF per bag sold = (P − v)(1 − T)
ΔNPV per bag = ΔOCF per bag × annuity factor

solution: Each bag adds (P − v)(1 − T) = 5.50 × 0.70 = $3.85 of OCF per year
Over 6 years at 11%: $3.85 × 4.230538 = 16.2876 of NPV per bag

errors.label: Ignored the tax factor (1 − T)
errors.explain: Extra contribution is taxed, so only (1 − T) of it reaches OCF.

errors.label: Reported the one-year OCF change
errors.explain: $23,100 is only one year's OCF loss; the shortfall repeats each year for 6 years, so discount with the annuity factor.

errors.label: Used a 5-year annuity factor
errors.explain: Use N = 6 for a 6-year project.

questions.explanation: Fixed costs do not depend on volume, so each lost bag costs only the contribution margin after tax: (14 − 8.5)(1 − 0.30) = $3.85 per year. Over 6 years at 11% that is 3.85 × 4.230538 = $16.29 of NPV per bag, so 6,000 bags cost about $97,725.

questions.stem: Boreal Coffee Roasters is evaluating a $360,000 roasting line for a 6-year project with no salvage. Base case: price $14.00 per bag, variable cost $8.50 per bag, 52,000 bags per year, fixed costs $140,000 per year. The CCA tax shield is treated as straight-line, so D = $60,000 per year. T = 30% and the required return is 11% per annum. Compare a selling price 5% below base with a variable cost 5% above base: by how much more NPV is lost under the price shock?

steps.label: NPV lost from a 5% price drop ($0.70 per bag)
NPV lost from a 5% variable-cost rise ($0.425 per bag)

errors.label: Assumed price and cost have the same NPV effect, so no difference
errors.explain: A $1 change in price and a $1 change in variable cost do have equal-size effects (Q(1 − T) × annuity factor), but a 5% change is $0.70 for price and only $0.425 for cost. Compare equal percentage changes.

errors.label: Ignored the tax factor (1 − T)
errors.explain: Both effects are after-tax; leaving out (1 − T) overstates the difference.

errors.label: Used the one-year OCF difference
errors.explain: $10,010 is the annual OCF difference; NPV counts it for all 6 years, so multiply by the annuity factor.

questions.explanation: Equal percentage changes make the comparison fair. The price shock removes $0.70 × 52,000 × 0.7 = $25,480 of OCF a year, the cost shock only $15,470, because price is the larger base number. Discounting the $10,010 annual gap at 11% for 6 years gives about $42,348.

questions.stem: A project team will run a sensitivity analysis on 8 uncertain inputs: one baseline run plus one "up" and one "down" run for every input. How many full DCF calculations are needed?

errors.label: Left out the baseline run
errors.explain: Eight up-runs and eight down-runs give 16, but the base case is also a full DCF calculation.

errors.label: Ran only one direction per input
errors.explain: Each input is flexed both up and down, so there are 2N flexed runs, not N.

errors.label: Counted one run per input
errors.explain: N counts the inputs, not the runs.

questions.explanation: Each of the 8 inputs gets an up-run and a down-run (16 runs), and there is one baseline: 2N + 1 = 17.

questions.stem: In the Boreal Coffee Roasters project (52,000 bags per year, T = 30%) the variable cost per bag rises by $1.00 and nothing else changes. By how much does each year's operating cash flow change? Enter a negative number for a decrease.

errors.label: Ignored the tax saving on the extra cost
errors.explain: The extra cost is deductible, so only (1 − T) of it reduces cash flow.

errors.label: Reported an increase
errors.explain: A higher variable cost lowers OCF, so the change is negative.

questions.explanation: A $1 rise in variable cost lowers pre-tax profit by $52,000; the tax shield recovers 30%, so OCF falls by $36,400 each year. Multiply by the annuity factor (4.230538) if you want the effect on NPV.

questions.stem: Boreal Coffee Roasters' base-case NPV is $148,510.65 (annual OCF $120,200; 6 years; R = 11%; T = 30%). Fixed costs are re-forecast to be $15,000 per year higher, with everything else unchanged. What is the new NPV?
questions.explanation: After-tax, the extra $15,000 costs 15,000 × 0.7 = $10,500 a year. Over 6 years at 11% that is 10,500 × 4.230538 = $44,420.65, so NPV = $148,510.65 − $44,420.65 = $104,090.00. Skipping (1 − T) understates the new NPV, skipping the annuity factor treats one year's loss as the total, and a plus sign treats a cost as a gain.

questions.stem: A model of Calgary Aero Parts gives NPV = $210,000 when 10,000 units are sold and NPV = $273,000 when 11,500 units are sold, with every other input at its base value. What is the sensitivity ΔNPV/ΔQ?
options: $42.00 per unit
$0.02 per unit
$5.48 per unit
$23.74 per unit
questions.explanation: Slope = (273,000 − 210,000) ÷ (11,500 − 10,000) = 63,000 ÷ 1,500 = $42 per unit. Inverting the ratio gives $0.02, dividing the NPV change by the new quantity gives $5.48, and dividing the new NPV by the new quantity gives $23.74; none of these is a change in NPV per change in quantity.

questions.stem: A sensitivity analysis will flex 9 uncertain inputs up and down around a base case. How many full DCF calculations does it need?
questions.explanation: 2N + 1 = 2(9) + 1 = 19. Eighteen forgets the base-case run, 10 counts only one direction per input, and 9 counts inputs instead of runs.

questions.stem: Scenario analysis in project evaluation means:
options: changing one input at a time while all the others stay at their base values
drawing every input at random thousands of times from a distribution
solving for the single input value at which NPV equals zero
changing several inputs together in a sensible, consistent way to build base, best and worst cases
questions.explanation: Scenario analysis moves several inputs at once to create sensible cases (for example sales up 10% and costs up 8%), usually a base, a best and a worst case. One at a time is sensitivity, random draws are simulation, and a zero crossing is NPV break-even.

questions.stem: Northern Lights Cinemas builds three cases for a new multiplex. In the best case attendance and ticket price are 12% above forecast while staffing and concession costs are 8% below. The worst case is the mirror image, and the third case is the forecast itself. This technique is:
options: scenario analysis
sensitivity analysis
simulation analysis
NPV break-even analysis
questions.explanation: Several inputs move together in a consistent story, giving best, base and worst cases: scenario analysis. Sensitivity would move attendance alone, then price alone.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts scenario analysis with simulation?
options: scenario analysis draws its inputs at random, while simulation uses three hand-picked cases
scenario analysis changes only one input, while simulation changes all of them at once
scenario analysis gives a distribution of NPV, while simulation gives only three NPV values
scenario analysis uses a few hand-picked consistent cases; simulation draws all inputs at random thousands of times
questions.explanation: A scenario analysis has a handful of named cases (typically base, best and worst), so it produces only a handful of NPVs. Simulation randomizes all inputs from distributions and produces an entire distribution.

questions.stem: In a scenario analysis, why is the change in OCF not proportional to the change in sales?
options: the discount rate rises whenever sales rise, which lowers the NPV
fixed costs do not move with volume, so cost per unit falls as units rise
depreciation is zero whenever the level of sales changes
variable costs are ignored in scenario analysis calculations
questions.explanation: The lecture's reason: we have fixed and variable costs, and the fixed costs are spread over the number of units produced. So a 10% change in sales changes OCF by more than 10% when fixed costs are significant.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT belong in the worst-case scenario of a typical project?
options: fixed costs lower than the base case
unit sales lower than the base case
selling price lower than the base case
variable cost per unit higher than the base case
questions.explanation: In the worst case sales and price fall while costs (variable and fixed) rise. Lower fixed costs would be favourable, so they belong in the best case.

questions.stem: A scenario analysis gives NPV = +$1.8M in the best case, +$0.4M in the base case and −$1.2M in the worst case. What can we conclude?
options: accept, because the best-case gain is bigger than the worst-case loss in dollars
the project could gain or lose a lot; scenarios show what can happen, not how likely each case is
reject, because the worst-case NPV is negative and so the project fails
the expected NPV is the simple average of the three, about +$0.33M, so accept
questions.explanation: Scenario analysis tells us what can happen and helps gauge the potential for disaster, but it does not by itself tell us whether to take the project. To go further we need probabilities for the cases; an equal-weight average assumes they are equally likely.

questions.stem: Why not keep adding scenarios until every possibility is covered?
options: each extra scenario changes the discount rate used for the others
accounting rules limit scenario analysis to three cases per project
more cases only show more possibilities and give no decision rule (paralysis of analysis)
extra scenarios always lower the base-case NPV when added
questions.explanation: No matter how many scenarios we run, all we learn are possibilities, some good and some bad. Beyond a handful of sensible cases the extra work adds little guidance.

questions.stem: In a best-case scenario, price and quantity are raised while variable costs and fixed costs are lowered.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A best case moves every input in its favourable direction: revenues up, costs down. The worst case is the reverse.

questions.stem: If every input in a scenario moves 10% in the favourable direction, NPV rises by exactly 10%.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Scenario results are not linear. Fixed costs do not scale with volume and the investment outlay does not change, so a 10% favourable move in each input changes OCF and NPV by very different percentages (in the textbook example the best-case NPV is several times the base case).

questions.stem: The base-case NPV of a project is positive and its worst-case NPV is negative. What extra information lets management compute an expected NPV across the three scenarios?
options: the probability of each scenario
the IRR of each scenario
the payback period of the base case
the sensitivity of NPV to each input
questions.explanation: Expected NPV = Σ p × NPV, so each case needs a probability, and the probabilities must sum to 1. IRRs, payback and sensitivities do not weight the cases.

questions.stem: With probabilities p_best, p_base and p_worst (summing to 1), the expected NPV across scenarios is:
options: (NPV_best + NPV_base + NPV_worst) ÷ 3 for any probabilities
p_best × NPV_best + p_base × NPV_base + p_worst × NPV_worst
NPV_base × (1 + the average percentage change of the inputs)
NPV_best − NPV_worst
questions.explanation: Expected value is the probability-weighted sum of the scenario NPVs. A simple average is correct only if the three cases are equally likely, and the other two options are not expected values at all.

questions.stem: Okotoks Trailer Works plans a new trailer line costing $900,000 over 4 years, with no salvage, and treats CCA as straight-line (D = $225,000 per year). T = 30% and the required return is 12% per annum. Base case: price $2,400 and variable cost $1,350 per trailer, 1,200 trailers per year, fixed costs $620,000 per year. In the worst-case scenario, price and quantity are each 10% below base, and variable and fixed costs are each 10% above base. What is the worst-case NPV?

errors.label: Lowered variable cost in the worst case
errors.explain: In the worst case every cost moves UP. Cutting variable cost by 10% is a favourable move.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield T·D
errors.explain: OCF = (S − C)(1 − T) + T·D. Dropping T·D = $67,500 a year overstates the loss.

errors.label: Scaled the base OCF down by 10%
errors.explain: The scenario changes four inputs and fixed costs do not scale, so OCF does not simply fall 10%; it collapses to $100,400.

questions.explanation: The worst case changes all four inputs the unfavourable way. Because fixed costs rise while contribution shrinks, EBITDA drops from $640,000 to $47,000 and OCF to $100,400, producing a large negative NPV of about −$595,050. The change is far from a 10% move.

questions.stem: Elbow River Brewing is considering a $420,000 canning line for a 5-year project with no salvage. CCA is treated as straight-line (D = $84,000 per year), T = 25% and the required return is 9% per annum. Base case: price $31.00 and variable cost $19.00 per case, 60,000 cases per year, fixed costs $310,000. In the best-case scenario quantity is 20% above base, price 5% above, variable cost 5% below and fixed costs 10% below. What is the best-case NPV?
keystrokes: TVM: N = 5, I/Y = 9, PMT = −1, CPT PV = 3.889651

errors.label: Raised variable cost 5% in the best case
errors.explain: In the best case costs move DOWN. Variable cost 5% above base is an unfavourable move.

errors.label: Raised fixed costs 10% in the best case
errors.explain: In the best case fixed costs fall by 10%, to $279,000, not rise to $341,000.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: OCF includes T·D = 0.25 × 84,000 = $21,000 a year from the tax shield.

questions.explanation: Best case means revenues up (price and quantity) and costs down (variable and fixed). EBITDA climbs from $410,000 in the base case to $765,000, OCF to $594,750, and NPV to about $1.89 million, much more than a 10% to 20% change.

questions.stem: Lac Ste. Anne Outfitters values a project in three scenarios: best case NPV = $1,350,000 (probability 20%), base case NPV = $410,000 (probability 50%) and worst case NPV = −$690,000 (probability 30%). What is the project's expected NPV?

errors.label: Used a simple average of the three NPVs
errors.explain: A simple average treats the three cases as equally likely; the probabilities here are 20%, 50% and 30%.

errors.label: Added the worst-case loss instead of subtracting it
errors.explain: The worst-case NPV is negative, so its weighted contribution is −$207,000.

errors.label: Reported the base-case NPV only
errors.explain: Expected NPV weights all three scenarios by their probabilities.

questions.explanation: Expected NPV is the probability-weighted sum of the scenario NPVs: 0.2(1,350,000) + 0.5(410,000) + 0.3(−690,000) = $268,000. The positive expected value does not remove the 30% chance of a $690,000 loss.

questions.stem: Okotoks Trailer Works plans a new trailer line costing $900,000 over 4 years, with no salvage, and treats CCA as straight-line (D = $225,000 per year). T = 30% and the required return is 12% per annum. Base case: price $2,400 and variable cost $1,350 per trailer, 1,200 trailers per year, fixed costs $620,000 per year. Optimistic scenario: sales 20% above forecast and, with extra supervisors, fixed costs 5% higher; price and variable cost per trailer unchanged. What is the scenario NPV?
solution: OCF rises 30.01% and NPV rises 70.6% for a 20% rise in sales: not linear.

errors.label: Scaled the base NPV up by 20%
errors.explain: Sales up 20% does not mean NPV up 20%. Fixed costs are spread over more units and the outlay is unchanged, so NPV rises far more (about 70.6%).

errors.label: Forgot the 5% rise in fixed costs
errors.explain: The scenario changes two inputs together: volume and fixed costs.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: OCF = (S − C)(1 − T) + T·D; the shield is $67,500 a year.

questions.explanation: A scenario changes several inputs together. Here volume +20% and fixed costs +5% lift EBITDA from $640,000 to $861,000 (+34.5%), OCF by about 30%, and NPV by about 70.6% because the $900,000 outlay does not change. This is why scenario results are not linear.

questions.stem: A project's base case is: price $50, variable cost $30 per unit, 10,000 units, fixed costs $100,000, CCA $40,000 a year and T = 40%. In the best-case scenario price and quantity are each 10% higher and variable and fixed costs are each 10% lower. What is the best-case annual OCF?
questions.explanation: Best case inputs: P = 55, v = 27, Q = 11,000, FC = 90,000. EBITDA = (55 − 27)(11,000) − 90,000 = 218,000; OCF = 218,000 × 0.6 + 0.4 × 40,000 = $146,800. Raising variable cost (107,200) or fixed cost (134,800) in the best case moves a cost the wrong way, and dropping the tax shield gives $130,800.

questions.stem: A project's NPV is estimated at $820,000 in the best case (probability 25%), $300,000 in the base case (45%) and −$560,000 in the worst case (30%). What is the expected NPV?
questions.explanation: E[NPV] = 0.25(820,000) + 0.45(300,000) + 0.30(−560,000) = 205,000 + 135,000 − 168,000 = $172,000. The equal-weight average is $186,666.67, the base case alone is $300,000, and attaching the probabilities to the wrong scenarios gives $241,000.

questions.stem: A project has 6 uncertain inputs. How many full DCF calculations are needed for a sensitivity analysis, and how many for a scenario analysis with a base, a best and a worst case?
options: 13 for sensitivity and 3 for scenario
12 for sensitivity and 2 for scenario
7 for sensitivity and 3 for scenario
13 for sensitivity and 6 for scenario
questions.explanation: Sensitivity needs 2N + 1 = 13 runs; a scenario analysis needs one run per case, so 3 no matter how many inputs there are. Twelve forgets the base case, 7 is N + 1, and 6 confuses the number of inputs with the number of cases.

questions.stem: Simulation analysis in capital budgeting is best described as:
options: changing one input at a time and recomputing NPV, for 2N + 1 runs in total
building a best, a base and a worst case by moving several inputs together
a computer drawing all uncertain inputs at random many times and studying the distribution of NPV
solving for the single input value that sets NPV equal to zero
questions.explanation: Simulation randomizes all inputs according to chosen distributions, repeats thousands of times, and then looks at the distribution of the output. The three distractors describe sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis and NPV break-even analysis.

questions.stem: Cedar Mills fits a triangular distribution to each of six uncertain inputs, has a spreadsheet draw a value for all six at once, computes the NPV, and repeats this 10,000 times. The analyst then plots a histogram of the 10,000 NPVs. This technique is:
options: sensitivity analysis
scenario analysis
NPV break-even analysis
simulation analysis
questions.explanation: Random draws from distributions for all inputs, repeated thousands of times, with a histogram of the NPV output, is simulation. Sensitivity moves one input at a time and scenario uses a few hand-picked consistent cases.

questions.stem: How does simulation analysis differ from scenario analysis?
options: scenario analysis changes one input at a time, while simulation changes several together
scenario analysis tries a few hand-picked combinations; simulation draws all inputs at random and gives a distribution of NPV
simulation produces a single accept or reject threshold, while scenario analysis produces a distribution
the two are identical and differ only in the software used
questions.explanation: A scenario analysis uses a handful of sensible, consistent cases (base, best, worst). Simulation randomizes every input from a distribution many times and yields the whole output distribution.

questions.stem: Why do we study the whole distribution of simulated NPVs rather than only the average?
options: the average of simulated NPVs is always wrong and must be replaced
only the single highest NPV matters for the accept decision
the distribution is always a normal curve centred on the base-case NPV
the shape shows how likely losses are and how skewed the outcomes are, which the average alone hides
questions.explanation: The professor stresses that the shape is important, not just the baseline: two projects with the same mean can have very different chances of NPV below zero. The output is usually not symmetrical and its peak need not sit at the base case.

questions.stem: A simulation of 8,000 trials gives a mean NPV of +$310,000, but 35% of the trials have a negative NPV. Which reading is best?
options: the mean is positive, but over a third of outcomes destroy value, so the downside matters, not only the mean
any negative trial proves the project must be rejected, whatever the mean is
the true NPV of the project is -35%, because 35% of trials are negative
the simulation shows that the base-case forecast was wrong and must be redone
questions.explanation: Simulation describes the range and likelihood of outcomes. A positive mean with a 35% chance of NPV below zero means substantial downside risk; it does not by itself prove rejection, and 35% is a probability of loss, not an NPV.

questions.stem: Which statement about the output distribution of a simulation is NOT necessarily true?
options: it is symmetrical, with its peak at the base-case NPV
its shape matters, not just its mean
it may be skewed to one side
it is built from many random draws of the inputs
questions.explanation: The lecture warns that the output distribution will probably not be symmetrical and that the baseline or expected value may not be at the peak. The other three statements are true.

questions.stem: Simulation analysis gives a simple decision rule that tells us whether to accept the project.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Simulation describes the range and likelihood of NPV outcomes, but no simple rule tells us what to do with them. Judgement about the downside is still needed.

questions.stem: Before a simulation can be run, the analyst must choose a probability distribution for each uncertain input.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The computer draws each input from the distribution the analyst chooses, so those distributions (and any links between inputs) are the key assumptions of the whole method.

questions.stem: Pacific Rail is evaluating a terminal with eight uncertain inputs (volume, price, fuel, wages and others). The board wants the probability that the project's NPV is negative. Which technique can supply it?
options: sensitivity analysis
scenario analysis with best, base and worst cases
simulation analysis
NPV break-even analysis on unit sales
questions.explanation: Only simulation produces a whole distribution of NPV, from which the share of negative outcomes can be read. Sensitivity flexes one input, scenarios give three points, and break-even gives one threshold.

questions.stem: Why should a realistic simulation model the relationships between inputs, such as price and quantity sold?
options: NPV cannot be calculated at all unless the inputs are correlated with each other
correlation between inputs makes every simulated NPV come out positive
inputs are not independent, and separate draws can produce combinations that never occur together
taxes are computed from the correlation between price and quantity sold
questions.explanation: If price and quantity tend to move together (or against each other), independent draws will generate unrealistic combinations and distort the NPV distribution. This is one reason simulation is hard to do well.

questions.stem: The textbook describes simulation analysis as an extension that combines:
options: payback analysis and discounted payback analysis, applied together
cash break-even analysis and accounting break-even analysis together
the capital asset pricing model and the capital market line
scenario analysis (many inputs change) and sensitivity analysis (many values)
questions.explanation: Scenario analysis lets all inputs change but only to a few values; sensitivity lets one input take many values. Letting all inputs take many values at once is a crude form of simulation.

questions.stem: In simulation analysis the analyst studies the _____ of the output NPV, not only its expected value.
options: payback
distribution
break-even
tax rate
questions.explanation: The point of simulation is the shape of the output: spread, skew and the chance of negative NPV. The baseline or expected value alone does not tell us that.

questions.stem: A simulation of a new project produces 5,000 NPV results, and 1,100 of them are negative. What percentage of the simulated outcomes have a negative NPV?

errors.label: Reported the share of positive trials
errors.explain: 3,900 of the 5,000 trials are positive (78%). The question asks for the negative ones.

errors.label: Divided by the positive trials only
errors.explain: The share of outcomes is out of all 5,000 trials, not out of the positive ones.

questions.explanation: The probability of a negative NPV is estimated by the share of simulated trials with NPV below zero: 1,100 out of 5,000 is 22%. This is the kind of statement simulation can make and the other what-if tools cannot.

questions.stem: A simulation's average NPV is $212,000, while the base-case NPV (all inputs at their expected values) is $240,000. Which explanation is possible?
options: the output distribution can be skewed, so its average need not equal the NPV computed at the average inputs
the simulation must contain a programming error, because the two numbers must always be equal
the base case ignored taxes, which is the only possible source of a difference
the simulation automatically used a higher discount rate
questions.explanation: The baseline or expected value may not be at the peak, and the output is probably not symmetrical, so the simulated mean can differ from the base-case NPV. A difference is not evidence of a mistake.

questions.stem: In one run of a simulation, what happens immediately after the computer draws a random value for every uncertain input?
options: the probability distribution for each input is chosen
the histogram of all the NPVs is summarized
the input is solved for the value that gives NPV = 0
the NPV for that set of inputs is computed and recorded
questions.explanation: The sequence is: choose distributions, draw all inputs, compute and record the NPV, repeat thousands of times, then summarize the distribution. Distributions are chosen before the first draw, and the summary comes after all runs.

questions.stem: Which is a typical weakness of simulation analysis?
options: it can only be used once the project's NPV is already known to be positive
it needs a distribution for every input and their relationships, which are hard to estimate
it can vary only one input at a time, so it misses combinations of inputs
it ignores the time value of money when computing each trial's NPV
questions.explanation: Simulation is limited by the quality of the assumed distributions and correlations, and by the lack of a simple decision rule. It still discounts cash flows in every run and varies all inputs at once.

questions.stem: NPV break-even analysis asks:
options: how far can an input change before NPV crosses zero and the accept decision flips
at what sales level accounting net income is exactly zero
what the NPV is when every input takes its best value
what the distribution of NPV looks like after thousands of random draws
questions.explanation: NPV break-even finds the input level at which NPV = 0, i.e. how far an input can move before the decision to accept would change. The distractors describe accounting break-even, best-case scenario and simulation.

questions.stem: NPV break-even (the finance version) differs from accounting break-even in that:
options: it ignores depreciation, while accounting break-even includes it
it sets NPV, not accounting profit, to zero, so it reflects the required return
its sales level is always lower than the accounting break-even sales level
it looks only at variable costs and ignores fixed costs
questions.explanation: Accounting break-even makes net income zero and ignores the required return. NPV break-even makes NPV zero, so it needs a higher level of sales for a normal project. Leaving out depreciation describes cash break-even, not NPV break-even.

questions.stem: A project's sales are above its accounting break-even level, so it reports a profit. Why can its NPV still be negative?
options: accounting profit already includes the cost of capital, so NPV counts it twice
accounting break-even uses fixed costs only, so it is always too low
accounting profit ignores the time value of money and the return investors require on the investment
NPV ignores depreciation entirely, which makes it lower
questions.explanation: A profit only says that revenues cover costs and depreciation. NPV also asks whether the cash flows earn the required return after discounting. A project can be profitable on paper and still destroy shareholder value.

questions.stem: At a planning meeting the CFO of Sunrise Bakeries asks: "By how much could our selling price fall before this project stops being worth doing?" Answering that question is:
options: NPV break-even analysis
scenario analysis
simulation analysis
accounting break-even analysis on sales volume
questions.explanation: She asks how far one input can move until the accept decision changes, i.e. until NPV reaches zero. That is NPV break-even. Scenario and simulation describe ranges of outcomes, and accounting break-even is about zero profit, not zero NPV.

questions.stem: A project's expected price is $9.40 and its NPV break-even price is $8.75, all else equal. Which interpretation is correct?
options: price can fall about 7.4% below the forecast before NPV reaches zero, which is a comfortable cushion
the project should be rejected because the break-even price is a positive number
accounting profit is zero when the price is $8.75, so the project breaks even on paper
price can fall about 6.9% below the forecast before NPV reaches zero; a thin cushion means high forecasting risk
questions.explanation: The cushion is (9.40 − 8.75) ÷ 9.40 = 0.65 ÷ 9.40 = 6.9% of the forecast price. Dividing by the break-even price gives 7.4%, the wrong base. NPV is still positive at $9.40, and NPV = 0 at $8.75 does not mean accounting profit is zero.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT true at the NPV break-even level of an input (all other inputs at their base values)?
options: the NPV equals zero
for conventional cash flows the IRR equals the required return
accounting net income equals zero
the accept or reject decision is exactly on the margin
questions.explanation: At NPV break-even, NPV = 0, IRR = R and the decision is on the margin. Net income is zero at the accounting break-even, a different and lower sales level.

questions.stem: At an input's NPV break-even level, the project's IRR equals the required return (for conventional cash flows).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. NPV = 0 at a discount rate R means that R is the IRR, so the IRR equals the required return at the NPV break-even.

questions.stem: NPV break-even analysis changes several inputs together to find the combination that makes NPV zero.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. NPV break-even solves for ONE input, holding the others at their base values, so that NPV = 0. Changing several inputs together is scenario analysis.

questions.stem: A plant costs I0. Its CCA tax shield is a level annuity of DTS for N years and its pre-tax operating income (EBITDA) is a level perpetuity. Which equation gives the break-even EBITDA?
options: −I0 + DTS × annuity factor(R, N) + EBITDA ÷ R = 0
−I0 + (1 − T) × EBITDA ÷ R = 0
−I0 + DTS × annuity factor(R, N) + (1 − T) × EBITDA × N = 0
−I0 + DTS × annuity factor(R, N) + (1 − T) × EBITDA ÷ R = 0
questions.explanation: The three components of NPV are the outlay, the PV of the DTS annuity and the PV of the after-tax perpetuity (1 − T)EBITDA ÷ R. Leaving out (1 − T) ignores tax, leaving out the DTS ignores the shield, and multiplying by N treats a perpetuity as N payments.

questions.stem: When solving for the break-even EBITDA, why do we divide the required after-tax cash flow by (1 − T)?
options: because the tax rate must be added to the discount rate in the perpetuity
EBITDA is pre-tax, and only (1 − T) of each pre-tax dollar remains after tax
because the CCA tax shield has to be taxed a second time as income
because EBITDA is measured after interest and depreciation have been deducted
questions.explanation: The NPV equation needs after-tax cash flow, which is (1 − T) × EBITDA. To find the pre-tax EBITDA that delivers a required after-tax amount we divide by (1 − T). Forgetting this step gives an answer that is too low.

questions.stem: On a sensitivity graph of NPV against selling price, the NPV line crosses zero at a price of $8.75. That price is called the project's:
options: accounting break-even price
cash break-even price
internal rate of return
NPV break-even price
questions.explanation: The price at which NPV crosses zero is the NPV (financial) break-even price. Accounting break-even sets net income to zero and cash break-even sets operating cash flow to zero; neither is where NPV is zero.

questions.stem: Base-case EBITDA for a plant is forecast at $312,000 a year and the NPV break-even EBITDA is $274,500. What does the analysis support?
options: accept, since EBITDA can fall about 12.0% before NPV reaches zero
accept, since EBITDA can fall about 13.7% before NPV reaches zero
reject, because the break-even EBITDA is above zero
no decision is possible without knowing the accounting break-even
questions.explanation: The forecast is above the break-even, so NPV is positive at the base case. The cushion is (312,000 − 274,500) ÷ 312,000 = 12.0% of the forecast. Dividing by the break-even gives 13.7%, the wrong base.

questions.stem: Glenmore Stamping will build a plant for $1,600,000. For simplicity CCA is treated as straight-line over 10 years, and the plant will then earn the same pre-tax operating income (EBITDA) every year forever. T = 30% and the discount rate is 8% per annum. What is the minimum EBITDA that gives NPV = 0?

steps.label: PV the income must supply = I0 − PV(DTS)

errors.label: Treated the required amount as pre-tax
errors.explain: EBITDA is pre-tax. The perpetuity pays (1 − T) × EBITDA after tax, so divide by (1 − T)/R, not just by 1/R.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: The shield is worth $322,084 of the outlay, so the income only has to supply the rest.

errors.label: Valued the 10-year shield as a perpetuity
errors.explain: The shield lasts only 10 years; use the annuity factor, not 1/R.

questions.explanation: Set NPV = 0: the outlay of $1,600,000 must be repaid by the CCA tax shield (a 10-year annuity worth about $322,084) and by the after-tax perpetuity (1 − T)EBITDA ÷ R = 8.75 × EBITDA. That leaves 8.75 × EBITDA = $1,277,916, so EBITDA is at least $146,047.55.

questions.stem: Pembina Packaging will buy a sealing line for $350,000 for a 5-year project with no salvage. CCA is treated as straight-line (D = $70,000 per year), T = 30% and R = 12% per annum. Volume is 25,000 units per year, variable cost is $18.00 per unit and fixed costs are $120,000 per year. What is the minimum unit price that gives NPV = 0?

steps.label: Required OCF for NPV = 0 (I0 ÷ annuity factor)
Required contribution per unit = (EBITDA + FC) ÷ Q

errors.label: Found the accounting break-even price (net income = 0)
errors.explain: At that price OCF equals D = $70,000, which only repays the outlay with no return. Accounting break-even ignores the 12% required return.

errors.label: Treated OCF − T·D as pre-tax EBITDA
errors.explain: OCF − T·D is an after-tax amount; divide it by (1 − T) to get the pre-tax EBITDA.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: OCF includes T·D = $21,000 from the shield, so the operations need to supply that much less.

questions.explanation: NPV = 0 requires a constant OCF of 350,000 ÷ 3.604776 = $97,093.41. Subtract the CCA shield (0.3 × 70,000 = 21,000) and gross up by 1 ÷ (1 − 0.3) to get EBITDA of $108,704.87. Add fixed costs, divide by 25,000 units and add the $18.00 variable cost to reach a price of about $27.15, well above the $25.60 accounting break-even price.

questions.stem: Wolf Willow Vineyards will plant a new block for $750,000. The investment earns no CCA tax shield, and it should earn the same pre-tax net cash revenue every year forever. T = 28% and the discount rate is 9% per annum. What is the minimum annual pre-tax net cash revenue that makes NPV = 0?

steps.label: Required after-tax cash flow = R × I0

solution: A perpetuity is worth C ÷ R, so NPV = −750,000 + (1 − T)·X ÷ R = 0
After-tax cash flow needed: C = R × I0 = 0.09 × 750,000 = $67,500

errors.label: Stopped at the after-tax amount
errors.explain: $67,500 is what must arrive after tax. The pre-tax figure must be larger so that 72% of it equals $67,500.

errors.label: Multiplied by (1 − T) instead of dividing
errors.explain: Tax takes a share of pre-tax revenue, so the pre-tax figure is the after-tax figure divided by (1 − T).

questions.explanation: With no tax shield and a perpetual flow, NPV = 0 needs (1 − T)X ÷ R = I0, so X = R × I0 ÷ (1 − T) = 0.09 × 750,000 ÷ 0.72 = $93,750.00.

questions.stem: Mackenzie Foods computes its project's NPV at two sales levels, with every other input at its base value: NPV = $412,000 at 80,000 units and NPV = $603,000 at 90,000 units. NPV is a straight-line function of units sold. At how many units sold does NPV equal zero?

steps.label: Slope ΔNPV/ΔQ in dollars per unit

solution: From 80,000 units, NPV must fall by $412,000: 412,000 ÷ 19.10 = 21,570.68 units

errors.label: Added the distance instead of subtracting
errors.explain: NPV is positive at 80,000 units and rises with volume, so the zero crossing lies below 80,000 units.

errors.label: Used the NPV change for 10,000 units as the slope per unit
errors.explain: $191,000 is the change over 10,000 units. Divide by 10,000 to get $19.10 per unit before solving.

questions.explanation: NPV is linear in units, so the slope is constant: $19.10 per unit. NPV is $412,000 at 80,000 units, so it reaches zero 412,000 ÷ 19.10 = 21,570.68 units lower, at about 58,429.32 units.

questions.stem: Kananaskis Snow Systems buys snow-making equipment for $900,000 for a 5-year project. The CCA rate is 30% with the half-year rule, T = 30% and the discount rate is k = 10% per annum. The equipment is sold for $120,000 at the end of year 5. Pre-tax operating income (EBITDA) is the same each year and there is no net working capital. Using the formula-sheet PV of the CCA tax shield with its salvage term, find the minimum annual EBITDA that gives NPV = 0.

steps.label: PV of the CCA tax shield (with salvage term)

errors.label: Used a first-year factor of 1 instead of (1 + 0.5k) ÷ (1 + k)
errors.explain: Under the half-year rule the first-year factor is (1 + 0.5k) ÷ (1 + k) = 0.9545, which lowers the PV of the shield.

errors.label: Divided by the annuity factor but not by (1 − T)
