errors.explain: The operations supply (1 − T) × EBITDA after tax, so the annuity factor must be multiplied by (1 − T).

errors.label: Dropped the salvage term from the PVCCA formula but kept the sale proceeds
errors.explain: When the asset is sold the pool loses S, so the later shield falls: subtract S·d·T ÷ (k + d) × 1 ÷ (1 + k)^N.

questions.explanation: NPV = 0 requires the operations to cover what the shield and the salvage do not: 900,000 − 176,530.58 − 74,510.56 = $648,958.86. That is the PV of a 5-year annuity of (1 − T) × EBITDA at 10%, so EBITDA = 648,958.86 ÷ (0.7 × 3.790787) = $244,562.45.

questions.stem: Cypress Hills Cabinets will buy a $420,000 machine for a 6-year project with no salvage. CCA is treated as straight-line (D = $70,000 per year), T = 30% and R = 11% per annum. Price is $40.00 per unit, volume is 30,000 units per year and fixed costs are $200,000 per year. What is the highest variable cost per unit at which NPV is still zero?

errors.label: Found the variable cost at which accounting profit is zero
errors.explain: At $31.00 net income is zero, but OCF then only equals D and earns no return. The NPV break-even variable cost is lower.

errors.label: Treated OCF − T·D as pre-tax EBITDA
errors.explain: Divide the after-tax amount by (1 − T) to get pre-tax EBITDA.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: OCF includes T·D = $21,000 from the shield; ignoring it demands too much from operations.

questions.explanation: A 6-year annuity at 11% must repay $420,000, so OCF must be at least $99,278.16. Strip out the shield (0.3 × 70,000) and gross up for tax to get EBITDA of $111,825.94. Adding fixed costs and dividing by 30,000 units gives a required contribution of $10.39 per unit, so variable cost can be at most $29.61.

questions.stem: Fort Saskatchewan Plastics buys a press for $500,000 and treats CCA as straight-line over 5 years. Pre-tax operating income (EBITDA) will be the same every year forever. T = 40% and R = 10% per annum. What is the minimum EBITDA for NPV = 0?
questions.explanation: DTS = 0.4 × 500,000 ÷ 5 = 40,000 a year; PV(DTS) = 40,000 × 3.790787 = 151,631.47. Then (1 − T) ÷ R = 6, so EBITDA = (500,000 − 151,631.47) ÷ 6 = $58,061.42. Stopping before dividing by (1 − T) gives $34,836.85, ignoring the shield gives $83,333.33, and valuing the shield as a perpetuity gives $16,666.67.

questions.stem: A $600,000 production line lasts 5 years with no salvage. CCA is treated as straight-line (D = $120,000 per year), T = 30% and R = 10% per annum. Each unit earns a contribution (price minus variable cost) of $20.00 and fixed costs are $150,000 per year. What annual sales volume gives NPV = 0?
options: 16,234 units
13,500 units
13,614 units
7,500 units
questions.explanation: OCF* = 600,000 ÷ 3.790787 = 158,278.49. EBITDA = (158,278.49 − 0.3 × 120,000) ÷ 0.7 = 174,683.55. Q = (150,000 + 174,683.55) ÷ 20 = 16,234 units. The accounting break-even is 13,500, forgetting ÷(1 − T) gives 13,614, and the cash break-even FC ÷ contribution is 7,500.

questions.stem: An investment of $480,000 will produce the same after-tax operating cash flow in each of 4 years. The required return is 14% per annum. What is the smallest annual OCF that gives NPV = 0?
questions.explanation: OCF* = I0 ÷ annuity factor(14%, 4) = 480,000 ÷ 2.913712 = $164,738.30. Dividing by N gives $120,000 (no return), treating the flow as a perpetuity gives $67,200, and using a 5-year factor gives $139,816.10.

questions.stem: At the cash break-even sales level, a project's _____ is exactly zero.
options: net income
NPV
payback period
operating cash flow
questions.explanation: Cash break-even sets OCF = 0, so Q_C = FC/(P − v). Net income = 0 is the accounting break-even (depreciation joins the numerator) and NPV = 0 is the financial break-even.

questions.stem: Kootenay Outfitters launches a new product line. At 9,000 units a year the line just covers its fixed operating costs in cash, but nothing is left over to repay the initial outlay. Which break-even point is this?
options: Cash break-even
Accounting break-even
Financial break-even
Payback break-even
questions.explanation: Covering the fixed cash costs and nothing more means OCF = 0, the cash break-even Q_C = FC/(P − v). Nothing is left to recover the outlay, so the IRR is −100%. Accounting break-even would at least return the depreciation (OCF = D), and financial break-even would also earn the required return.

questions.stem: Fraser Valley Kayaks plans a paddleboard line. The price is $64.50 per board, variable cost is $38.20 per board, fixed costs are $412,000 a year and depreciation is $165,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the cash break-even quantity (boards per year)?
solution: Contribution margin P − v = 64.50 − 38.20 = $26.30 per board
Cash break-even: OCF = 0, so Q_C = FC/(P − v) = 412,000/26.30 = 15,665.40 boards per year

errors.label: Added depreciation to the numerator
errors.explain: That is the accounting break-even. Depreciation is not a cash cost, so it stays out of the cash break-even.

errors.label: Divided fixed costs by the price
errors.explain: Each board contributes P − v = $26.30 toward fixed costs, not the whole price.

errors.label: Divided fixed costs by the variable cost
errors.explain: The denominator is the contribution margin P − v, not the variable cost per unit.

questions.explanation: Cash break-even is the sales level where OCF = 0: Q_C = FC/(P − v). Depreciation is not a cash cost, so it plays no part (that is why the $165,000 is a distractor).

questions.stem: Peace River Pottery sells mugs for $46.80. Each mug costs $11.35 in labour, $7.90 in clay and glaze and $1.25 in packaging. Fixed costs are $385,000 a year and depreciation is $140,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the cash break-even quantity?
options: 19,962 mugs
13,975 mugs
14,639 mugs
8,226 mugs
questions.explanation: Total variable cost is v = 11.35 + 7.90 + 1.25 = $20.50, so P − v = $26.30 and Q_C = 385,000/26.30 = 14,639 mugs. Adding the $140,000 of depreciation gives 19,962 (the accounting break-even), and dropping packaging from v overstates the margin and understates the break-even.

questions.stem: Algoma Canoe sells a model for $1,240 with a variable cost of $815 per canoe. The project's cash break-even is 538 canoes a year. What annual fixed costs does that imply?
solution: Q_C = FC/(P − v) rearranges to FC = Q_C × (P − v)

errors.label: Multiplied Q_C by the price
errors.explain: Only the contribution margin P − v covers fixed costs, so FC = Q_C × (P − v), not Q_C × P.

errors.label: Multiplied Q_C by the variable cost
errors.explain: That is total variable cost at the break-even volume, not the fixed costs.

errors.label: Divided Q_C by the margin
errors.explain: The formula is FC/(P − v) = Q_C, so FC is the product Q_C × (P − v), not the quotient.

questions.explanation: Rearrange Q_C = FC/(P − v) to FC = Q_C × (P − v). At the break-even volume the total contribution exactly equals fixed costs.

questions.stem: Okanagan Cider Works prices a new line at $58.00 a case with a variable cost of $33.50. Fixed costs are $310,000 a year and depreciation is $120,000 a year. The tax rate is 30%, and any tax loss on this project can be used against the firm's other income. At what quantity is OCF exactly zero?
solution: OCF = [(P − v)Q − FC](1 − T) + T·D; set OCF = 0

errors.label: Subtracted T·D but did not divide by (1 − T)
errors.explain: The shield sits after tax while the numerator is pre-tax, so it must be grossed up by 1/(1 − T).

errors.label: Ignored taxes: FC/(P − v)
errors.explain: With taxes the depreciation shield still produces cash when the pre-tax result is negative, which lowers the cash break-even.

errors.label: Added the grossed-up shield instead of subtracting it
errors.explain: At OCF = 0 the shield replaces some of the fixed cost burden, so it is subtracted from FC.

questions.explanation: With taxes, OCF = [(P − v)Q − FC](1 − T) + T·D. Setting it to zero gives Q_C = {FC − T·D/(1 − T)}/(P − v) = 10,553.94, below FC/(P − v) = 12,653.06 because the depreciation tax shield is still earned when pre-tax profit is negative.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts cash break-even with accounting break-even?
options: Cash break-even includes the required return on the investment; accounting break-even does not
Cash break-even leaves depreciation out of the numerator; accounting break-even includes it
Cash break-even is the higher of the two quantities for a project with positive depreciation
Cash break-even sets net income to zero; accounting break-even sets operating cash flow to zero
questions.explanation: Q_C = FC/(P − v) covers only cash fixed costs; Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) also covers depreciation, so Q_A > Q_C. The required return belongs to financial break-even, and the claim that cash break-even sets net income to zero swaps the roles of net income and OCF.

questions.stem: Which statement about a project operating exactly at its cash break-even point is NOT true?
options: Operating cash flow is zero in every year
The IRR is −100%
The payback period equals the project's life
The NPV equals minus the initial outlay
questions.explanation: At cash break-even no cash comes back, so the project never pays back, the IRR is −100% and NPV = −I0. Payback exactly equal to the life describes the accounting break-even, where OCF = D.

questions.stem: Why is the cash break-even quantity always below the accounting break-even quantity when a project has positive depreciation?
options: Cash break-even uses the after-tax contribution margin, which is larger
Cash break-even discounts the fixed costs, which makes the numerator smaller
Cash break-even leaves out variable costs, which makes the denominator larger
Depreciation is not a cash cost, so cash break-even only has to cover the cash fixed costs
questions.explanation: Q_A adds D to the numerator, and D is an accounting charge rather than a cash outflow. Discounting enters only the financial break-even (and raises it), and variable costs sit in the denominator of all three.

questions.stem: Tri-City Print's new line has a cash break-even of 8,000 units a year, and management forecasts sales of 7,400 units. What does this tell management?
options: Operating cash flow is negative, so the line needs cash just to keep running
Net income is zero, so the line earns its depreciation in cash
NPV is zero, so the line earns exactly its required return
The line pays back its outlay in exactly its useful life
questions.explanation: Sales below Q_C mean (P − v)Q < FC, so OCF < 0. That is worse than the accounting break-even case, where OCF at least equals depreciation. Zero NPV and payback equal to life describe other break-even points.

questions.stem: Lakeland Foods has spare capacity. A one-time order for 5,000 jars is offered at $2.60 a jar. Variable cost is $2.05 a jar, the $480,000 of fixed costs is paid whether or not the order is accepted, and the average cost is $3.10 a jar. What should it do?
options: Reject: $2.60 is below the average cost of $3.10 a jar
Accept: the $0.55 contribution per jar adds $2,750 to cash flow and fixed costs are paid anyway
Reject: the order must also cover its share of the $480,000 of fixed costs
Accept only if the price exceeds $3.10, so the order shows an accounting profit
questions.explanation: Fixed costs are effectively sunk for this choice, so only the marginal cost (v = $2.05) matters: 5,000 × (2.60 − 2.05) = $2,750 of extra cash. Average cost includes fixed costs that do not change, which is why it misleads.

questions.stem: In Q_C = FC/(P − v), fixed costs rise by 20% and the contribution margin P − v also rises by 20%. What happens to the cash break-even quantity?
options: It rises by 20%
It rises by 44%
It is unchanged
It falls by 20%
questions.explanation: Both the numerator and the denominator are multiplied by 1.20, so Q_C = 1.20 FC/(1.20 (P − v)) is unchanged. A 20% rise in only FC would lift Q_C by 20%, and a 44% rise has no basis in the formula.

questions.stem: When taxes are ignored, a project's cash break-even quantity does not depend on its depreciation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Q_C = FC/(P − v) has no D in it. Depreciation affects the accounting break-even Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v), not the cash break-even.

questions.stem: Mapleview Bikes' project has fixed costs of $1,020,000 a year and a variable cost of $310 per bike. At a price of $480 its cash break-even is 6,000 bikes. If the price is raised to $520 with costs unchanged, what is the new cash break-even?
options: 4,857 bikes
1,962 bikes
4,588 bikes
5,538 bikes
questions.explanation: The contribution margin rises from $170 to $210, so Q_C = 1,020,000/210 = 4,857 bikes. Dividing by the whole price (1,962) ignores variable cost, cutting 6,000 by the 23.5% rise in the margin (4,588) treats Q_C as linear in the margin, and scaling 6,000 by the price ratio (5,538) treats Q_C as proportional to 1/P. Q_C = FC/(P − v) must be recomputed with the new margin.

questions.stem: At the accounting break-even sales level, a project's _____ is exactly zero.
options: operating cash flow
NPV
net income
payback period
questions.explanation: Accounting break-even sets net income (and so EBIT and taxes) to zero: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v). Operating cash flow equals depreciation at that point, not zero.

questions.stem: At 4,600 units a year the income statement of a new line shows EBIT of zero, no taxes and net income of zero, while operating cash flow equals the annual depreciation. Which break-even point is this?
options: Cash break-even
Financial break-even
Payback break-even
Accounting break-even
questions.explanation: Net income = 0 defines accounting break-even. Since OCF = NI + D, OCF = D there, which is positive; at cash break-even OCF would be zero and at financial break-even NPV would be zero.

questions.stem: Cariboo Trailers will invest $2,640,000 in equipment, depreciated straight-line to zero over 8 years. Fixed costs are $845,000 a year, the price is $31.40 per unit and variable cost is $18.65 per unit. Ignoring taxes, what is the accounting break-even quantity (units per year)?

errors.label: Left depreciation out (used FC only)
errors.explain: That is the cash break-even. Accounting break-even must cover depreciation too.

errors.label: Added the whole investment instead of one year's depreciation
errors.explain: Only the annual charge D = I0/N belongs in the numerator.

errors.label: Divided by the price instead of P − v
errors.explain: The denominator is the contribution margin P − v, not the price.

questions.explanation: Accounting break-even is where net income is zero: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) with D = I0/N for straight-line to zero. Taxes do not matter because taxable income is zero there.

questions.stem: Yellowhead Signage plans a project with price $27.50, variable cost $16.20 and fixed costs of $520,000 a year. It needs a $1,350,000 investment, depreciated straight-line to zero over 6 years. The required return is 10%; ignore taxes. If sales sit exactly at the accounting break-even each year, what is the NPV?

errors.label: Treated zero profit as zero NPV
errors.explain: Accounting break-even makes net income zero, but the investment is only recovered with no return, so NPV is negative.

errors.label: Set OCF to zero (cash break-even)
errors.explain: At accounting break-even OCF equals depreciation, not zero; the flows of $225,000 are still worth something.

errors.label: Used a 5-year annuity factor
errors.explain: The project lasts 6 years, so the annuity factor must use N = 6.

questions.explanation: At accounting break-even OCF = D = I0/N each year, so NPV = I0[(1/N) × annuity factor − 1]. With any positive required return that is negative: the project returns the money invested but never the time value (IRR = 0%).

questions.stem: Yukon Snowmobile Parts has a price of $212 and a variable cost of $139 per unit. Fixed costs are $1,460,000 a year. It invests $5,600,000 in equipment, depreciated straight-line to zero over 7 years, and expects operating cash flow of $1,200,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the accounting break-even quantity?
options: 36,438 units
20,000 units
30,959 units
96,712 units
questions.explanation: D = 5,600,000/7 = $800,000, so Q_A = (1,460,000 + 800,000)/73 = 30,959 units. The $1,200,000 of operating cash flow is a lure: at accounting break-even OCF equals D, not the base-case OCF. Using FC alone gives the cash break-even and using the whole investment overstates the charge.

questions.stem: A project must reach accounting break-even at 12,500 units a year. Fixed costs are $288,000, depreciation is $96,000 and variable cost is $14.80 per unit. What selling price achieves that?
questions.explanation: Solve Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) for P: P = (FC + D)/Q_A + v = 384,000/12,500 + 14.80 = $45.52. Leaving out v gives only the contribution margin of $30.72, omitting D lowers the price to $37.84, and subtracting v moves the wrong way.

questions.stem: Prairie Window Systems has a price of $410, variable cost of $268, fixed costs of $390,000 and depreciation of $150,000 a year; the tax rate is 32%. Use OCF = NI + D at the break-even, then Q = {FC + (OCF − T·D)/(1 − T)}/(P − v), to find the accounting break-even quantity.
solution: NI = 0 at accounting break-even, so OCF = NI + D = $150,000
Q_A = 540,000/142 = 3,802.82 units, identical to (FC + D)/(P − v)

errors.label: Divided the margin by (1 − T) as well
errors.explain: No tax is paid at accounting break-even, so there is nothing to gross up in the denominator.

errors.label: Used after-tax depreciation D(1 − T)
errors.explain: Depreciation is a pre-tax charge in the break-even condition; the shield was already handled by the general formula.

errors.label: Multiplied the whole numerator by (1 − T)
errors.explain: At zero profit the tax rate cancels completely, so the numerator is just FC + D.

questions.explanation: Because OCF = D at accounting break-even, (OCF − T·D)/(1 − T) = D(1 − T)/(1 − T) = D, so Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) whatever the tax rate. The tax rate is a distractor.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts accounting break-even with financial break-even?
options: Accounting break-even charges the opportunity cost of capital; financial break-even does not
Accounting break-even sets net income to zero and ignores the time value of money; financial sets NPV to zero
Accounting break-even is always higher than financial break-even, because depreciation is included
The two are equal whenever the project has no salvage value
questions.explanation: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) recovers the investment with no return, while Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v) uses the OCF* that earns the required return, so for a normal project Q_F > Q_A.

questions.stem: Which statement about a project operating exactly at its accounting break-even point is NOT true?
options: Net income is zero
Taxes paid are zero
The project's NPV is zero
Operating cash flow equals depreciation
questions.explanation: At accounting break-even EBIT, taxes and net income are zero and OCF = NI + D = D. The investment comes back with no return (IRR = 0%), so NPV is negative at any positive required return.

questions.stem: Why is clearing the accounting break-even not enough to justify accepting a project?
options: It counts depreciation as a cash outflow, which makes NPV look worse than it is
It includes interest expense, which does not belong in project cash flows
It ignores variable costs, so the quantity it gives is too low
At accounting break-even the IRR is zero, so NPV is negative at any positive required return
questions.explanation: Accounting break-even earns only the depreciation back (OCF = D, payback equal to the life). Without a return on the money tied up, NPV = I0[(1/N) × annuity factor − 1] < 0. That is why we also need the financial break-even.

questions.stem: Muskoka Skiff Co. finds an accounting break-even of 44 skiffs a year against a sales forecast of 58. A director says, "We clear break-even by 14 skiffs, so the project is safe." What is the best response?
options: Clearing accounting break-even says nothing about NPV, so compute the financial break-even
Agree: any project forecast above accounting break-even has a positive NPV
Agree: above accounting break-even the IRR must exceed the required return
Disagree: the project must still reach its cash break-even before it is safe
questions.explanation: Sales above Q_A keep net income positive, but the IRR only exceeds zero, not necessarily the required return. Since Q_F > Q_A, a forecast of 58 skiffs could still fall short of Q_F. Cash break-even is lower than Q_A, so clearing Q_A already clears it.

questions.stem: Which change would lower a project's accounting break-even quantity, all else equal?
options: Buying more equipment that raises straight-line depreciation
A cut in annual fixed costs
A lower selling price
A higher variable cost per unit
questions.explanation: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v): smaller FC shrinks the numerator, while more depreciation raises it and a lower P or higher v shrinks the contribution margin in the denominator.

questions.stem: A pricier machine adds $50,000 to annual straight-line depreciation. Fixed cash costs and the contribution margin of $12.50 per unit are unchanged. What happens to the break-even quantities?
options: Q_A rises by 4,000 units and Q_C rises by 4,000 units
Q_A falls by 4,000 units and Q_C is unchanged
Q_A rises by 4,000 units and Q_C is unchanged
Both are unchanged, because depreciation is not a cash cost
questions.explanation: ΔQ_A = ΔD/(P − v) = 50,000/12.50 = 4,000 units, and it is a rise because D sits in the numerator. Q_C = FC/(P − v) contains no depreciation, so it is unchanged. Depreciation does matter to Q_A even though it is not a cash cost.

questions.stem: For a project depreciated straight-line to zero, operating at its accounting break-even every year gives a payback period equal to the project's life and an IRR of zero.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: At accounting break-even OCF = D = I0/N each year, so the cash flows add up to exactly I0 over N years: payback = N and IRR = 0%.

questions.stem: Algonquin Candles sells candles at $18.50 with a variable cost of $7.25 each. Fixed costs are $196,000 a year and depreciation is $59,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what annual sales revenue is needed to reach the accounting break-even?

errors.label: Used the cash break-even quantity
errors.explain: That leaves depreciation out; the accounting break-even must cover FC + D.

errors.label: Reported total contribution (FC + D) as revenue
errors.explain: FC + D is the contribution needed, not the sales revenue; revenue is P × Q_A.

errors.label: Multiplied the quantity by the variable cost
errors.explain: Revenue is quantity × price, not quantity × variable cost.

questions.explanation: Find Q_A first, then convert to dollars with the price. At revenue of $419,333.33, variable costs are $164,333.33, fixed costs $196,000 and depreciation $59,000: EBIT = 0.

questions.stem: Why does the tax rate not appear in Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v)?
options: Taxes are paid only on cash flows, and operating cash flow is zero at that point
Net income is zero there, so no tax is paid and the rate drops out
Taxes are already included in the fixed costs FC
The depreciation tax shield exactly cancels tax on revenue at every sales level
questions.explanation: Net income = (S − VC − FC − D)(1 − T) = 0 requires S − VC − FC − D = 0 whatever T is, so dividing by (1 − T) removes it. At that point OCF = D, not zero.

questions.stem: A project has an accounting break-even of 4,400 units a year, a price of $85, a variable cost of $52 and fixed costs of $90,000 a year. Its equipment is depreciated straight-line to zero over 5 years. What initial investment does this imply?

steps.label: Annual depreciation D = Q_A(P − v) − FC

solution: Q_A = (FC + D)/(P − v) rearranges to D = Q_A(P − v) − FC

errors.label: Did not subtract fixed costs when solving for D
errors.explain: The break-even quantity covers FC + D, so D is what is left after fixed costs.

errors.label: Reported one year's depreciation as the investment
errors.explain: Straight-line depreciation is I0/N, so the investment is N times the annual charge.

questions.explanation: Work backwards: D = Q_A(P − v) − FC = $55,200, and with straight-line depreciation to zero over 5 years the investment is I0 = 5D = $276,000.

questions.stem: At the financial break-even sales level, a project's _____ is exactly zero.
options: net income
operating cash flow
NPV
payback period
questions.explanation: Financial break-even is the sales level that makes NPV = 0, so the project earns exactly its required return. Net income = 0 is the accounting break-even and OCF = 0 is the cash break-even.

questions.stem: Sault Boatworks finds that at 3,200 boats a year its project's IRR equals the 12% required return and its discounted payback equals the six-year life. Which break-even point has it found?
options: Accounting break-even
Cash break-even
Payback break-even
Financial break-even
questions.explanation: IRR = R, NPV = 0 and discounted payback equal to the life all describe the financial break-even. Accounting break-even would give IRR = 0% and payback equal to the life, and cash break-even gives IRR = −100%.

questions.stem: Yoho Gear is evaluating a $412,000 project with a 5-year life. Fixed costs are $96,000 a year, the price is $37.80 and variable cost is $24.30 per unit. The required return is 11% and depreciation is straight-line to zero. Ignoring taxes, what is the financial break-even quantity (units per year)?
solution: NPV = 0 means I0 = OCF* × annuity factor, so OCF* = I0 ÷ [(1 − 1.11^−5)/0.11]

errors.label: Used I0/N as the required OCF
errors.explain: I0/N is the depreciation, so that is the accounting break-even. OCF* must also earn the required return: divide by the annuity factor.

errors.label: Used the whole investment as one year's OCF
errors.explain: The investment is the PV of the OCF annuity, not one year's OCF; divide by the annuity factor.

errors.label: Left OCF* out (cash break-even)
errors.explain: That sets OCF = 0. Financial break-even needs OCF* large enough to give NPV = 0.

questions.explanation: Financial break-even: find OCF* that makes the PV of the annuity equal I0, then Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v). The order cash (7,111) < accounting (13,215) < financial (15,369) holds.

questions.stem: Cranbrook Cabinets has a price of $240 and a variable cost of $162 per unit, with fixed costs of $410,000 a year. A $1,500,000 investment is depreciated straight-line to zero over its 5-year life. The tax rate is 35% and the required return is 14%. What is the financial break-even quantity (units per year)?

errors.label: Did not divide (OCF* − T·D) by (1 − T)
errors.explain: OCF* is after tax but FC and the margin are pre-tax, so the after-tax gap OCF* − T·D must be grossed up by 1/(1 − T).

errors.label: Ignored taxes: (FC + OCF*)/(P − v)
errors.explain: With a 35% tax rate the firm must earn extra pre-tax income to pay tax, so the no-tax formula understates the break-even.

errors.label: Added T·D instead of subtracting it
errors.explain: The depreciation tax shield supplies part of OCF*, so it reduces what the operations must produce.

questions.explanation: With taxes the OCF identity is OCF = [(P − v)Q − FC](1 − T) + T·D. Solving for Q at OCF = OCF* gives Q_F = {FC + (OCF* − T·D)/(1 − T)}/(P − v). Forgetting the ÷(1 − T) understates Q_F by about 2,300 units.

questions.stem: A project has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $31 per unit and a 4-year life with straight-line depreciation to zero. Its cash break-even is 9,600 units and its accounting break-even is 13,000 units. The required return is 13%; ignore taxes. What is the financial break-even quantity (units)?

steps.label: Annual depreciation D = Q_A(P − v) − FC
Required OCF* = I0 ÷ annuity factor (13%, 4 years)

errors.label: Used I0/N as the required OCF
errors.explain: I0/N = D, which just reproduces the accounting break-even (13,000). OCF* needs the annuity factor.

errors.label: Took one year's D as the investment
errors.explain: Straight-line depreciation is I0/N, so I0 = 4D = $340,000.

errors.label: Used a 5-year annuity factor
errors.explain: The project lasts 4 years, so the annuity factor must use N = 4.

questions.explanation: Work backwards through Q_C and Q_A to P − v, D and I0, then find OCF* from the annuity factor. The three answers 9,600 < 13,000 < 14,172 confirm the order cash < accounting < financial.

questions.stem: Thompson Valley Distillery has a price of $92 and a variable cost of $57 per case, with fixed costs of $310,000 a year. A $1,900,000 investment is depreciated straight-line to zero over 8 years. The required return is 9% and taxes are ignored. What is the financial break-even quantity?
options: 15,643 cases
8,857 cases
19,643 cases
18,665 cases
questions.explanation: The annuity factor (9%, 8 years) is 5.5348, so OCF* = 1,900,000/5.534819 = $343,281 and Q_F = (310,000 + 343,282)/35 = 18,665 cases. Using I0/N = $237,500 gives the accounting break-even (15,643), and using no OCF* gives the cash break-even (8,857).

questions.stem: Bruce Peninsula Canoes earns a contribution margin of $11.50 per canoe and has fixed costs of $150,000 a year. A $780,000 investment is depreciated straight-line to zero over 6 years, the required return is 15% and taxes are ignored. What is the financial break-even quantity?
options: 269,730 canoes
24,348 canoes
13,043 canoes
None of the above
questions.explanation: OCF* = 780,000/3.784483 = $206,105 and Q_F = (150,000 + 206,105)/11.50 = 30,966 canoes, which none of the listed figures equals. Multiplying by the annuity factor, using I0/N (the accounting figure, 24,348) and ignoring OCF* (the cash figure, 13,043) are the classic slips.

questions.stem: How does the financial break-even quantity compare with the cash break-even quantity?
options: Financial break-even is lower, because discounting shrinks the cash flows
Financial break-even is higher, because OCF must also repay I0 at the required return
The two are equal, because both set operating cash flow to its break-even level
Financial break-even is lower, because it ignores fixed costs
questions.explanation: Q_C = FC/(P − v) needs OCF = 0, while Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v) needs OCF* > 0 to give NPV = 0. Discounting raises the OCF required; it does not shrink it.

questions.stem: Which statement about a project operating exactly at its financial break-even point is NOT true?
options: Its NPV is zero
Its IRR equals the required return
Its ordinary payback exceeds its life
Its discounted payback equals its life
questions.explanation: At financial break-even the PV of the OCFs just equals I0, so NPV = 0, IRR = R and discounted payback = life. Undiscounted flows add up to more than I0, so ordinary payback is shorter than the life, not longer.

questions.stem: Why is the financial break-even the most important of the three for shareholders?
options: It is the lowest of the three, so a project is most likely to pass it
It ignores the time value of money, which keeps the analysis simple
It is unaffected by forecasting risk in the sales volume
A project can clear the other two break-evens yet still have a negative NPV
questions.explanation: Only Q_F = (FC + OCF*)/(P − v) ties the sales level to NPV = 0. Forecast sales above Q_C and Q_A but below Q_F still destroy value. Q_F is the highest of the three, not the lowest.

questions.stem: Selkirk Vineyards has a financial break-even of 3,010 bottles a year against a sales forecast of 3,100. What does this tell management?
options: The NPV is positive only if sales hold within about 3% of the forecast, so forecasting risk is high
The project is safe, because the forecast is above the break-even level
The NPV is exactly zero, because the break-even is so close to the forecast
The project pays back in exactly its life, so the IRR is zero
questions.explanation: Margin of safety = (3,100 − 3,010)/3,100 ≈ 2.9%. NPV is positive at the forecast, but a small miss in volume wipes it out. This is the point the text makes about the Wettway sailboat project.

questions.stem: For a project with an initial outlay, positive depreciation and a positive required return, which ordering of the three break-even quantities is always correct?
options: Cash < financial < accounting
Cash < accounting < financial
Accounting < cash < financial
Financial < accounting < cash
questions.explanation: Q_C = FC/(P − v), Q_A adds D, and Q_F adds OCF*, which is larger than D because OCF* must repay I0 with interest. So Q_C < Q_A < Q_F.

questions.stem: A project's price, costs, depreciation and investment stay the same but its required return rises. What happens to the three break-even quantities?
options: All three rise
Q_C, Q_A and Q_F are all unchanged
Q_C and Q_A are unchanged and Q_F rises
Q_F falls, because the annuity factor falls
questions.explanation: The required return enters only through OCF* = I0 ÷ annuity factor. A higher rate lowers the annuity factor, so OCF* and Q_F rise. The annuity factor falling does not lower Q_F, since it is in the denominator of OCF*.

questions.stem: Pacific Rim Tiles' project has Q_C = 7,100, Q_A = 13,200 and Q_F = 15,400 units a year, and sales are forecast at 14,500 units. What follows?
options: Accept: forecast sales exceed the accounting break-even, so the project earns a profit and a positive NPV
Accept: operating cash flow is positive, which is all that matters
Reject: the forecast is below the accounting break-even
It clears Q_C and Q_A but not Q_F, so NPV is negative: reject unless other value is found
questions.explanation: Only the financial break-even is tied to NPV. Forecast 14,500 < Q_F = 15,400 means OCF is below OCF*, so NPV < 0 even though accounting profit and OCF are positive.

questions.stem: At the financial break-even quantity, a project's IRR equals its required return.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Financial break-even is NPV = 0, and the IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero, so IRR = R at that sales level.

questions.stem: The degree of operating leverage is DOL = 1 + _____ ÷ OCF.
options: fixed costs plus depreciation
variable costs
fixed costs
depreciation
questions.explanation: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF. A common slip is to put depreciation into the numerator as well; D is already inside OCF and is not part of the leverage ratio.

questions.stem: A project's operating cash flow rises 14% when the quantity sold rises 5%. What does the ratio 14%/5% = 2.8 measure?
options: The profitability index
The internal rate of return
The contribution margin
The degree of operating leverage
questions.explanation: DOL is defined by %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ, so the ratio %ΔOCF/%ΔQ is the project's degree of operating leverage (2.8 here).

questions.stem: Bow Valley Signs expects fixed costs of $215,000 and operating cash flow of $96,400 at its forecast volume. Depreciation is $48,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is the project's degree of operating leverage?

errors.label: Added depreciation to fixed costs
errors.explain: Depreciation is not part of the leverage ratio; the numerator is FC alone.

errors.label: Dropped the 1
errors.explain: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF. With zero fixed costs DOL is 1, not 0.

errors.label: Inverted the ratio
errors.explain: The ratio is fixed costs divided by OCF, not OCF divided by fixed costs.

questions.explanation: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF = 1 + 215,000/96,400 = 3.23: each 1% change in quantity moves OCF by 3.23%. The $48,000 of depreciation is a distractor.

questions.stem: A project has a degree of operating leverage of 2.65 at 18,000 units a year. Volume rises to 19,500 units. By what percentage does operating cash flow rise?

errors.label: Used DOL − 1 as the multiplier
errors.explain: The multiplier is DOL itself: %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ.

errors.label: Divided %ΔQ by DOL
errors.explain: Leverage magnifies: OCF changes by DOL times the percentage change in quantity.

errors.label: Gave the answer as a decimal instead of a percent
errors.explain: The answer box is in %, so 0.2208 must be written as 22.08.

questions.explanation: %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ = 2.65 × 8.33% = 22.08%. Because OCF is linear in Q, this relationship is exact for any size of change, though DOL itself then falls.

questions.stem: Prince George Tire has a degree of operating leverage of 3.40 at 48,000 tires a year, and fixed costs of $210,000. Ignoring taxes, volume falls to 43,000 tires. What is the new degree of operating leverage?

errors.label: Kept the old DOL of 3.40
errors.explain: DOL depends on the current OCF; when volume falls, OCF falls and FC/OCF rises, so DOL rises.

errors.label: Cut OCF in proportion to volume
errors.explain: OCF falls by DOL × %ΔQ (35.4%), not by %ΔQ (10.4%), because fixed costs do not fall.

errors.label: Raised OCF instead of cutting it
errors.explain: Volume fell, so %ΔQ is negative and OCF falls.

questions.explanation: Back out OCF from the DOL, apply %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ, then recompute DOL on the lower OCF. Operating leverage rises as volume falls, so the project becomes more fragile.

questions.stem: Thunder Bay Cabinets sells 12,000 units a year at $150 with a variable cost of $90. Fixed costs are $480,000 and depreciation is $75,000 a year. Ignoring taxes, what is its degree of operating leverage?
questions.explanation: Without taxes OCF = (P − v)Q − FC = 60 × 12,000 − 480,000 = $240,000, so DOL = 1 + 480,000/240,000 = 3.00. Adding D to FC gives 3.31, using EBIT (after the $75,000 depreciation) as if it were OCF gives 3.91, and dropping the 1 gives 2.00.

questions.stem: Muskoka Spa Covers earns operating cash flow of $150,000 at 20,000 units a year and has fixed costs of $330,000. If volume falls 10% (ignoring taxes), what is the new operating cash flow?
questions.explanation: DOL = 1 + 330,000/150,000 = 3.2, so %ΔOCF = 3.2 × (−10%) = −32% and new OCF = 150,000 × 0.68 = $102,000. Cutting OCF only 10% ignores the fixed costs, which do not fall with volume.

questions.stem: Kelowna Kitchenware has fixed costs of $648,000 a year and a $1,120,000 investment depreciated straight-line to zero over 7 years. Ignoring taxes, what is the degree of operating leverage when it sells exactly the accounting break-even quantity?
solution: At accounting break-even NI = 0, so OCF = NI + D = D = $160,000

errors.label: Added depreciation to fixed costs
errors.explain: The numerator is FC alone; D appears only as the OCF in the denominator at this special point.

errors.label: Dropped the 1
errors.explain: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF.

errors.label: Used the whole investment as OCF
errors.explain: OCF equals one year's depreciation (I0/N), not the whole investment.

questions.explanation: At accounting break-even OCF = D, so DOL = 1 + FC/D = 5.05. A 1% rise in volume above break-even lifts OCF by 5.05%: leverage is highest near break-even.

questions.stem: Two plans for the same product both earn operating cash flow of $400,000 at forecast volume. Plan X (in-house production) has fixed costs of $600,000 a year; Plan Y (subcontracting) has fixed costs of $120,000. Which statement is correct?
options: Plan Y has the higher DOL, because its fixed costs are lower
The DOLs are equal, because both plans earn the same OCF
Plan X has DOL 2.5 against 1.3 for Plan Y, so its OCF is more exposed
Plan X has the lower DOL, because it earns more per unit sold
questions.explanation: DOL_X = 1 + 600/400 = 2.5 and DOL_Y = 1 + 120/400 = 1.3. Equal OCF does not mean equal leverage: DOL depends on FC/OCF, so the plan with the heavier fixed costs has more forecasting risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of a high degree of operating leverage?
options: Small percentage changes in volume cause large percentage changes in operating cash flow
Errors in the sales forecast are magnified in the cash flow forecast
Break-even quantities tend to be higher
Operating cash flow becomes more stable when sales volume fluctuates
questions.explanation: High fixed costs magnify volume swings in OCF (%ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ), raise forecasting risk and push the break-even points up. Stability of OCF is the opposite of what leverage does.

questions.stem: Why does a project's degree of operating leverage fall as the quantity sold rises?
options: OCF grows with volume while fixed costs stay put, so FC/OCF shrinks
Variable costs per unit fall as volume grows
The contribution margin per unit shrinks as volume grows
Depreciation per unit falls, which lowers the numerator
questions.explanation: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF. OCF = (P − v)Q − FC rises with Q, while FC is constant, so FC/OCF and DOL decline (the text's sailboat: DOL 2.0 at 50 boats, 1.5 at 75).

questions.stem: A project's degree of operating leverage is 4.5 at its forecast volume. What does this mean?
options: Each 1% change in units sold changes operating cash flow by 0.45%
Each 1% change in units sold changes operating cash flow by 4.5%
Operating cash flow is 4.5 times the fixed costs
The project breaks even at 4.5 times the forecast volume
questions.explanation: %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ = 4.5 × 10% = 45%. Since DOL = 1 + FC/OCF, FC/OCF = 3.5, so fixed costs are 3.5 times OCF, not the other way round.

questions.stem: Muskoka Cycles can make frames in-house (DOL 1.85 at forecast volume) or subcontract them (DOL 1.25). The two plans have similar NPVs, and management fears its sales forecast is too optimistic. Which plan is better?
options: In-house: the higher DOL protects OCF if volume falls short
Subcontract: a lower DOL guarantees a higher NPV
Subcontract: the lower DOL means a volume forecasting error is magnified less in OCF
Either: once NPVs are equal, operating leverage does not affect forecasting risk
questions.explanation: With NPVs level, the plan with lower operating leverage is less exposed to forecasting error: a 10% volume miss cuts OCF by about 12.5% rather than 18.5%. Low DOL lowers risk; it does not raise NPV.

questions.stem: What is the degree of operating leverage of a project with zero fixed costs?
options: It is undefined
questions.explanation: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF = 1 + 0 = 1: percentage changes in quantity pass one for one into OCF, so there is no magnification.

questions.stem: A project's degree of operating leverage stays the same whatever quantity is sold.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF depends on the current OCF. As Q rises, OCF rises and DOL falls (the text's sailboat: 2.0 at 50 boats, 1.5 at 75). The relationship %ΔOCF = DOL × %ΔQ holds from the starting point.

questions.stem: Selkirk Boats sells 5,000 boats a year at $1,450 with a variable cost of $892 per boat. Fixed costs are $2,050,000 and depreciation is $310,000 a year. Ignore taxes. Using the DOL, what is operating cash flow if volume rises 8%?

errors.label: Raised OCF by only 8%
errors.explain: Fixed costs do not rise with volume, so OCF rises by DOL × 8%, not 8%.

errors.label: Dropped the 1 from the DOL
errors.explain: DOL = 1 + FC/OCF; the 1 is the part of the swing that is not leverage.

errors.label: Added depreciation to fixed costs in the DOL
errors.explain: Depreciation is not part of FC in the leverage ratio.

questions.explanation: OCF = (P − v)Q − FC = $740,000, DOL = 3.77, so +8% volume raises OCF by about 30.2% to $963,200. The direct check (558 × 5,400 − 2,050,000) gives the same result, confirming DOL is exact for OCF.

questions.stem: A real option is the right, but not the _____, to undertake a business initiative in the future.
options: premium
probability
obligation
discount
questions.explanation: An option is a right, not an obligation: the holder decides in the future, using information not yet available, whether to act. If action were compulsory it would be a commitment, not an option.

questions.stem: Which statement defines an option?
options: A binding contract to carry out a business activity on a fixed future date
A forecast of project cash flows under best, base and worst cases
A probability-weighted average of the NPVs of several projects
A right, but not an obligation, to do something in the future
questions.explanation: The lecture defines an option as a right (but not an obligation) to act later, once more is known. A binding contract is a commitment, a three-case forecast is scenario analysis and a probability-weighted average is an expected value.

questions.stem: Atlantic Bakery builds its new plant with extra foundations and utility connections so that it can add a second production line later if demand proves strong. Which type of real option is this?
options: Expansion
Abandonment
Timing
Production flexibility
questions.explanation: Paying a little more now so that output can be increased later is the expansion option (the lecture's bigger machine or extra space). Abandonment is the right to exit early, and timing is the right to choose when to act.

questions.stem: A start-up trucking firm negotiates a clause that lets it resell its rigs at an agreed price after year 2 if its routes prove unprofitable. Which type of real option does the clause create?
options: Expansion
Abandonment
Timing
Production flexibility
questions.explanation: The right to exit a project early if it is not performing is the abandonment option, and the agreed resale price puts a floor under its value. Nothing in the clause adds capacity (expansion) or changes when the firm acts (timing).

questions.stem: A brewery can launch a canned seltzer this spring, or wait a year to see whether a rival's launch succeeds and then decide. What type of real option is the right to wait?
options: Expansion
Abandonment
Timing
Production flexibility
questions.explanation: Choosing the best time to act, after more information arrives, is the timing option (the lecture's example is the best time to replace a machine). Waiting does not add capacity or end an existing project.

questions.stem: A Saskatchewan fertilizer plant is built so that it can switch its output between two product grades as relative prices change. What type of real option is this?
options: Expansion
Abandonment
Timing
Production flexibility
questions.explanation: Being able to change the rate or type of production according to the market is production flexibility. The plant stays in operation, so this is neither abandonment nor expansion.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a financial option with a real option?
options: A financial option is a right to buy or sell an asset; a real option is a right to undertake a business activity
A financial option carries an obligation to exercise; a real option does not
A financial option has a premium; a real option is always free
A real option must be exercised on a fixed date; a financial option may lapse
questions.explanation: Both are rights without obligations and both usually cost something up front (the premium). They differ in what the right is about: a financial asset, or a business initiative.

questions.stem: How do the option to expand and the option to abandon differ in the way they add value?
options: Expansion limits the loss when things go badly; abandonment captures more upside
Expansion captures more upside when things go well; abandonment limits the loss when they go badly
Both lower the project's risk by cutting off its upside
Expansion is a financial option while abandonment is a real option
questions.explanation: Expansion is a call-like right to do more if the news is good; abandonment is a put-like right to sell the assets if the news is bad. Both are real options and neither cuts off the upside.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a real option?
options: The right to enlarge a plant later if demand turns out strong
The right to sell a project's assets early if it performs badly
A best, base and worst-case table of NPVs for different sales forecasts
The right to postpone a launch until more is known
questions.explanation: A scenario table changes inputs together to show the range of NPVs; it gives the firm no right to do anything. The other three are the expansion, abandonment and timing options.

questions.stem: Why does ignoring real options tend to understate a project's NPV rather than overstate it?
options: Options raise the discount rate, which lowers the NPV of a fixed plan
Option premiums are tax deductible, so ignoring them lowers cash flows
A fixed-plan DCF gives too much weight to the best case
An option is used only when it pays, so it can only add value, and a fixed-plan DCF leaves it out
questions.explanation: Because the firm uses an option only when it pays, it cannot make the project worse and often makes it better. A static DCF assumes the plan is fixed and values none of that flexibility (SM: ignoring the option to abandon underestimates NPV).

questions.stem: Why do we usually pay a premium up front to hold an option?
options: The right without the obligation is valuable, because the holder uses it only when it pays
The premium is the NPV the project is expected to earn
The premium compensates the seller for the holder's obligation to exercise
The premium is the resale value of the assets if the option is exercised
questions.explanation: Car insurance is the lecture's example. The point is that the right is worth money, so the person who grants it must be compensated. The challenge is to value the option, that is, to find a fair premium for the risk.

questions.stem: A project's static NPV is −$0.8 million. Analysts value its option to expand at $1.3 million. How should the result be interpreted?
options: The project is worth −$0.8 million and should be rejected, because the option cannot be counted
The project including its option is worth $0.5 million, so it is worth undertaking
The project is worth $2.1 million, found by subtracting the static NPV from the option value
The project is worth $1.3 million, because the option replaces the static NPV
questions.explanation: The option adds to the static value: −0.8 + 1.3 = +$0.5 million. Dropping the option leaves the NPV too low, and the option does not replace the static NPV or enter with the wrong sign.

questions.stem: A highway authority can build bridges sized for two lanes, or pay more now for longer bridges that make a later widening to three lanes cheap. How should the extra up-front cost of the longer bridges be viewed?
options: As a sunk cost that should be ignored
As a financing cost that should be excluded from the project
As the premium paid for a real option to expand the road later
As a side effect on the existing bridges
questions.explanation: Paying more now to keep the right to expand cheaply later is exactly the purchase of an expansion option (the lecture's freeway bridges). It is a new, avoidable cost, not a sunk or financing item.

questions.stem: When we value a real option, what do we assume about the future decision date?
options: That the firm will follow the original plan whatever it learns
That the firm will exercise the option in every state of the world
That the firm will choose the branch with the highest probability
That the firm will make the best financial decision given the information available then
questions.explanation: An option is valued by assuming the firm uses the right only when it is worth using. That is what lets us decide at each later node first and then work backwards (decision trees).

questions.stem: How is the value of a real option measured?
options: Project value with the flexibility minus value without it
The premium the firm pays up front to obtain it
The best-case NPV minus the worst-case NPV
The probability of exercise times the base-case NPV
questions.explanation: A real option's value is what the flexibility adds: NPV with the option minus NPV without. The premium is its price, which should not exceed that value. The best-minus-worst gap is a range, not an option value.

questions.stem: In the freeway bridges example, in which order do the events occur?
options: Learn whether the road is busy or quiet, then choose the bridges, then decide whether to widen
Choose short or long bridges, then learn whether the road is busy or quiet, then decide whether to widen
Decide whether to widen, then choose the bridges, then learn whether the road is busy or quiet
Choose the bridges, then decide whether to widen, then learn whether the road is busy or quiet
questions.explanation: Today's decision is the bridges, the unknown arrives next (busy or quiet, with probabilities), and the future decision (widen or not) comes last, once the information is known. That timeline is why we solve the tree from the last decision backwards.

questions.stem: A real option obliges the firm to carry out the business activity if conditions turn favourable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: An option is a right, not an obligation. The firm decides later, using the then-available information, whether to exercise.

questions.stem: Standard NPV analysis based on expected cash flows tends to ignore the value of managerial options.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A fixed-plan DCF values the expected flows of one plan and puts no value on the right to expand, abandon, wait or switch later. That is why options are analysed separately, for example with decision trees.

questions.stem: Muskoka Cycles can subcontract its frame production now or build an in-house plant. Subcontracting has a slightly lower NPV, but if sales boom the firm can start producing in-house later. Why might it still choose to subcontract?
options: Lower operating leverage plus an option to move production in-house later, which NPV omits
Real options never add value, so the lower NPV is a mistake
Subcontracting has no fixed costs, so it can never lose money
Choosing the plan with the lower NPV maximizes shareholder wealth
questions.explanation: The text notes that it is much easier to increase operating leverage later (buy equipment) than to reduce it. The lower DOL and the option to expand are worth something that the static NPV omits, though the choice should rest on a value comparison.

questions.stem: The lecture describes a car insurance policy as a put option. In that example, what is the option's premium?
options: The deductible
The price paid for the policy
The payout after a claim
The value of the car
questions.explanation: The premium is what we pay up front for the right. Here it is the cost of the policy; the payout is what the right is worth if it is used.

questions.stem: To solve a decision tree we start at the _____ decision node and work back to today.
options: earliest
most likely
latest
cheapest
questions.explanation: The later decision determines the value that flows back to the earlier node, so we decide at the latest node first and then probability-weight on the way back.

questions.stem: In a decision-tree diagram, "the road will be busy with probability 80% and quiet with probability 20%" is shown at which kind of node?
options: A decision node, valued by taking the best branch
A terminal node, valued by discounting its payoff
A decision node, valued by averaging its branches
A chance node, valued by probability-weighting its branches
questions.explanation: Nature, not the firm, chooses between busy and quiet, so the node carries probabilities and is valued as Σp × V. A decision node is where the firm chooses and takes the best branch, never an average.

questions.stem: Prairie Cold Storage must choose between a compact warehouse ($9.5M) and an expandable one ($12.8M). Demand will be high (probability 0.65) or low (0.35). If high, the compact building needs a $7.2M add-on and the expandable one only $2.6M; leaving high demand unserved costs $10.8M in lost margin. If low, nothing more is spent. All amounts are present values. What is the expected total cost today of the cheaper design, in $ millions?

steps.label: Compact, high-demand node: cheaper of add-on $7.2M or lost margin $10.8M
Expandable, high-demand node: cheaper of add-on $2.6M or lost margin $10.8M

solution: Decide at the latest node first: if demand is high, add on (7.2 < 10.8 for compact; 2.6 < 10.8 for expandable); if low, spend nothing
The lower expected cost is the compact design: $14.18 million (the amounts are already present values, so no further discounting)

errors.label: Averaged add-on and lost-margin costs before choosing
errors.explain: At the high-demand node the firm picks the cheaper branch; averaging $7.2M and $10.8M pretends it might leave demand unserved.

errors.label: Used 0.35 as the chance of the add-on
errors.explain: The add-on happens when demand is high, which has probability 0.65.

errors.label: Reported the expandable design's cost
errors.explain: The question asks for the cheaper design; the compact building costs less in expectation.

questions.explanation: Solve backwards: at each high-demand node choose the cheaper branch, then probability-weight. Compact costs $14.18M against $14.49M for expandable, so compact is cheaper by $0.31M in expected terms.

questions.stem: Bayview Brewing can run a $1.8M pilot of a new line. If demand proves strong (probability 0.35), a national rollout has an NPV of +$9.6M; if weak (0.65), rollout would have an NPV of −$4.2M, so the firm would decline it. Rollout NPVs are present values before the pilot cost and already reflect Bayview's 10% required return. What is the expected NPV of running the pilot, in $ millions?

steps.label: Expected value of the rollout opportunity

solution: Decide first at the weak-demand node: declining (0) beats rolling out (−4.2)
Pilot value = 3.36 − 1.8 = $1.56 million; the NPVs are already present values, so no more discounting

errors.label: Rolled out in the weak state too
errors.explain: The firm would decline the rollout when demand is weak, so that branch is worth 0, not −4.2.

errors.label: Discounted the NPVs again at 10%
errors.explain: The branch values are already present values; discounting again counts the time value twice.

errors.label: Left out the $1.8M pilot cost
errors.explain: The pilot is the up-front price of the rollout option and must be subtracted.

questions.explanation: Choose at the latest node first (decline when weak), then probability-weight the branches and subtract the pilot cost. The positive $1.56M shows the pilot's option to roll out is worth more than its cost.

questions.stem: Cedar Foods can test-market a new line for $1.0M. With probability 0.5 the test passes; the firm then chooses between a regional launch (NPV $3.2M for sure) and a national launch (probability 0.6 of $9.0M, probability 0.4 of −$2.0M). If the test fails, it stops. All NPVs are present values before the test cost. What is the test-market worth today, in $ millions?

steps.label: Expected value of the national launch
Decision node after a pass: larger of regional 3.2 and national
Expected value of the test outcomes

solution: Decision after a pass: national (4.6) beats regional (3.2), so carry back 4.6

errors.label: Took the sure regional launch
errors.explain: The national launch has the higher expected value (4.6 versus 3.2); at a decision node the firm takes the larger value.

errors.label: Averaged the two launch options
errors.explain: A decision node takes the best branch; averaging 3.2 and 4.6 treats the choice as random.

errors.label: Ignored the $1.0M test cost
errors.explain: The test cost is paid today whatever the outcome.

questions.explanation: Work from the right: the national chance node (4.6) feeds the decision node, which picks the better of 4.6 and 3.2; only then probability-weight the test outcome and subtract the cost.

questions.stem: Gulf Islands Resorts can invest now (NPV +$3.0M) or wait a year for demand to become clear. If demand is good (probability 0.6), investing then has a present-value NPV of $6.5M; if poor (0.4), it would be −$2.5M, so the firm would not invest. These are present values at a 10% required return. How much more is waiting worth than investing now, in $ millions?

steps.label: Poor-demand decision node: do not invest

solution: Decide at the poor-demand node first: not investing (0) beats −2.5
Extra value of waiting = 3.9 − 3.0 = $0.90 million (no discounting: the values are present values)

errors.label: Invested in the poor state too
errors.explain: If demand is poor the firm will not invest, so that branch is 0; including −2.5 makes waiting look worse than investing now.

errors.label: Discounted the waiting value again
errors.explain: The NPVs are already present values, so no further discounting is needed.

errors.label: Reported the value of waiting without subtracting NPV now
errors.explain: The question asks how much more waiting is worth than investing now: subtract the $3.0M.

questions.explanation: Waiting lets the firm avoid the poor-demand loss, so it is worth $3.9M against $3.0M now. The $0.90M difference is the value of the timing option.

questions.stem: Wolf Creek's overpass can be built narrow ($85M) or wide ($110M). Traffic will be heavy (probability 0.7) or light (0.3). If heavy, the narrow overpass needs a $30M rebuild and the wide one a $12M widening; doing nothing would cost society $90M. If light, nothing more is spent. All amounts are present values. What is the expected total cost of the cheaper design?
options: $106.0 million
$118.4 million
$127.0 million
$115.0 million
questions.explanation: At the heavy-traffic node the cheaper action is the rebuild ($30M, not $90M). Narrow: 85 + 0.7 × 30 = $106.0M; wide: 110 + 0.7 × 12 = $118.4M. Averaging $30M with $90M, or adding the rebuild with certainty, gives wrong totals.

questions.stem: Kodiak Energy pays $5.0M for a drilling lease. With probability 0.4 it finds oil worth $14.0M; with probability 0.6 the well is dry, and the firm then either sells the lease for $1.5M or spends $3.0M on a deeper well (probability 0.2 of $9.0M, 0.8 of nothing). All amounts are present values. What is the lease's expected NPV today?
options: $0.69 million
$1.50 million
−$0.12 million
$0.60 million
questions.explanation: At the dry-hole node the deeper well is worth 0.2 × 9.0 − 3.0 = −$1.2M, so the firm sells the lease for $1.5M. Then NPV = −5.0 + 0.4 × 14.0 + 0.6 × 1.5 = $1.50M. Averaging the two choices, or drilling deeper, gives wrong answers; ignoring the dry branch drops the lease sale.

questions.stem: A compact warehouse costs $9.5M and an expandable one $12.8M. If demand turns out high (probability p), the compact building needs a $7.2M add-on and the expandable one $2.6M; if demand is low, neither needs one. Amounts are present values. At what probability of high demand are the two designs equally costly? Answer in %.

steps.label: Extra up-front cost of the expandable design
Add-on saving if demand is high

solution: p* = 71.74%: above it the expandable design is cheaper, below it the compact one

errors.label: Divided the saving by the premium
errors.explain: The premium is paid for sure and the saving arrives with probability p, so p = premium/saving. This answer exceeds 100%.

errors.label: Ignored the $2.6M add-on on the expandable design
errors.explain: The saving is the difference between the two add-ons, 7.2 − 2.6 = 4.6.

errors.label: Reported the probability of low demand
errors.explain: p is the probability of high demand, which is when the add-on is needed.

questions.explanation: The extra $3.3M is a premium paid for sure; the saving of $4.6M arrives only with probability p. The designs tie where p × 4.6 = 3.3, so the expandable (option) design pays only if high demand is more than about 72% likely.

questions.stem: How does a decision tree differ from scenario analysis?
options: A decision tree changes several inputs together; scenario analysis models the firm's later choices
A decision tree uses random draws from distributions; scenario analysis uses probabilities
A decision tree ignores probabilities; scenario analysis requires them
A decision tree models the firm's later choices after uncertainty resolves; scenario analysis just changes inputs together
questions.explanation: Scenario analysis shows the NPV under best, base and worst combinations but assumes the firm sticks to its plan. A decision tree assigns probabilities and lets the firm respond at later decision nodes, which is where option value comes from.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of solving a decision tree?
options: Averaging the outcomes of a later decision node before choosing between its branches
Choosing the best branch at the latest decision node first
Probability-weighting the branch values at each chance node
Comparing the values of today's alternatives and picking the best
questions.explanation: At a decision node the firm picks the best branch; only chance nodes are averaged. Averaging first would assume the firm chooses at random, the classic averaging-before-deciding error.

questions.stem: Why do we start at the latest decision node and work back toward today?
options: Later cash flows are larger, so they should be valued first
The best later choice sets the value carried back to the earlier node
Probabilities are only known at the end of the tree
Discounting must always start from the final year
questions.explanation: What we do today depends on what we expect to do after the uncertainty resolves. So we value the last decisions first, using the best action at each, and carry those values back through the chance nodes.

questions.stem: In the professor's decision-tree examples, why do we not discount the branch values again?
options: Decision trees ignore the time value of money entirely
The branch probabilities already include the discount rate
They are already present values, so discounting again would double-count
Only cash flows beyond year 5 are ever discounted
questions.explanation: The slide states that the amounts are all NPVs, already discounted, which makes the tree easier. If the values were undiscounted future cash flows we would need DCF first, but we never discount a present value twice.

questions.stem: In a warehouse tree (compact $9.5M, expandable $12.8M; high demand with probability 0.65; add-on $7.2M versus $2.6M) the expected costs are $14.18M and $14.49M. What does this say about the expandable design's extra $3.3M?
options: The premium is worth paying because the add-on is cheaper if demand is high
The premium is a sunk cost and should be ignored
The expandable design wins because its worst-case cost is lower
It buys expected savings of only 0.65 × $4.6M = $2.99M, so it is not worth paying
questions.explanation: The comparison is on expected cost. The expandable design has the lower cost when demand is high (15.4 versus 16.7), but that happens only 65% of the time and saves $4.6M, so the expected saving of $2.99M falls short of the $3.3M premium.

questions.stem: At the post-pass decision node of a tree, a regional launch is worth $3.2M and a national launch has an expected value of $4.6M. What value is carried back to the node before it?
options: $4.6M, the larger of the two
$3.9M, the average of the two
$3.2M, the safer choice
$7.8M, the sum of the two
questions.explanation: A decision node takes the best branch, so the value carried back is the maximum, $4.6M. Averaging treats the choice as random, the safer option ignores the higher expected value, and the sum has no meaning.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the steps for solving a decision tree in the right order?
options: Write end-of-branch values, probability-weight every chance node, take the best branch at the latest decision node, compare today's alternatives
Write end-of-branch values, take the best branch at the latest decision node, probability-weight the chance nodes, compare today's alternatives
Take the best branch at the earliest decision node, write end-of-branch values, probability-weight the chance nodes, compare today's alternatives
Compare today's alternatives, write end-of-branch values, take the best branch at the latest decision node, probability-weight the chance nodes
questions.explanation: Start with the values at the ends, resolve the latest decision by taking the best branch, carry that value back through the chance nodes, and only then compare today's alternatives. Averaging before deciding is the standard error.

questions.stem: A planner lists today's choice (short or long bridges), the unknown future (a busy or quiet road, with probabilities) and a later decision (whether to widen). Which analysis tool is this?
options: Sensitivity analysis
Simulation analysis
Decision tree
NPV break-even analysis
questions.explanation: A decision tree combines a choice today, an uncertain future with probabilities and a future decision. Sensitivity changes one input at a time, simulation draws random inputs, and NPV break-even solves for the input that makes NPV zero.

questions.stem: A chance node has three branches worth $8.0M (probability 0.2), $3.0M (probability 0.5) and −$2.0M (probability 0.3). What is the expected value at the node?
options: $3.0 million
$3.1 million
$9.0 million
$2.5 million
questions.explanation: Expected value = Σ p × V = 1.6 + 1.5 − 0.6 = $2.5M. The simple average (3.0) ignores the probabilities, dropping the loss branch gives 3.1, and summing the values gives 9.0.

questions.stem: The probabilities on the branches leaving a chance node must add to 1.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A chance node covers every possible outcome, so its probabilities sum to 1 (for example 80% busy and 20% quiet). A decision node has no probabilities.

questions.stem: Timber Ridge Homes buys land for $2.0M. Rezoning is approved (probability 0.5), partly approved (0.3) or denied (0.2). Approved: build (PV $6.0M) or resell (PV $3.0M). Partly approved: build $2.2M or resell $2.6M. Denied: build −$1.1M or resell $0.4M. Values are present values before the land cost. What is the expected NPV of buying the land, in $ millions?

steps.label: Approved node: best of build 6.0 and resell 3.0
Partly approved node: best of build 2.2 and resell 2.6
Denied node: best of build −1.1 and resell 0.4
Expected value before the land cost
Expected NPV of buying the land

solution: Decide at each later node first: build (6.0) when approved, resell (2.6) when partly approved, resell (0.4) when denied

errors.label: Built in every outcome
errors.explain: At each later node the firm picks the better action; building when partly approved or denied is worse than reselling.

errors.label: Resold in every outcome
errors.explain: When approved, building (6.0) beats reselling (3.0).

errors.label: Left out the $2.0M land price
errors.explain: The land price is paid today and must be subtracted.

questions.explanation: Choose the best action at each rezoning outcome (build, resell, resell), probability-weight those values to 3.86 and subtract the land price. The flexibility to resell is what lifts the value above the always-build figure of $1.44M.

questions.stem: The option to _____ lets a firm commit more capital later, if the project is going well, to capture extra upside.
options: abandon
delay
expand
hedge
questions.explanation: The expansion option is the right to do more (bigger plant, extra space) once good news arrives. Abandonment limits losses and timing chooses when to act.

questions.stem: Maritime Wind Energy installs the grid connection and land lease for 12 more turbines at little extra cost, and will build them only if the first phase earns well. Which real option is this?
options: Option to abandon
Option to delay (timing)
Production flexibility
Option to expand
questions.explanation: Preparing now so that capacity can be added later if results are good is the expansion option. It is exercised only in the good outcomes, which is why it is a right and not an obligation.

questions.stem: Rocky Mountain Drilling Tools earns $128 after tax per unit sold each year. At the end of year 1 the project can be sold for $1,900,000; if kept, it runs 12 more years (years 2 to 13) at annual volume Q. The discount rate is 11%. Below what annual quantity Q is abandoning at the end of year 1 the better choice?

steps.label: PV at the end of year 1 per unit of Q: 128 × annuity factor
Abandonment threshold Q* = 1,900,000 ÷ PV per unit

solution: Abandon when the PV of continuing is below the resale value: 128 × Q × annuity factor(11%, 12) < 1,900,000
Annuity factor (11%, 12 years) = 6.492356; 128 × 6.492356 = 831.02 per unit of Q

errors.label: Used 13 years in the annuity factor
errors.explain: The later flows run in years 2 to 13, which is 12 payments valued at the end of year 1.

errors.label: Spread the resale value evenly instead of using an annuity factor
errors.explain: That ignores the time value of money; the flows must be valued with the annuity factor.

errors.label: Divided the resale value by one year's flow per unit
errors.explain: One year of flow per unit is not the value of 12 years of flows; multiply by the annuity factor.

questions.explanation: Abandon when the continuation value falls below the resale value. Setting 128 × Q × AF = 1,900,000 gives the break-even volume Q* = 2,286.34; below it the project is worth more sold. Both sides are measured at the end of year 1.

questions.stem: Cedar Mill Timber's project has a 0.4 probability of success (NPV +$8.5M) and a 0.6 probability of failure (NPV −$3.8M if it keeps running). If it fails, the firm can abandon and limit the NPV to −$1.6M. NPVs are present values today. What is the value of the abandonment option, in $ millions?

errors.label: Used the gain in the failure state without weighting it
errors.explain: The gain of $2.2M arises only with the failure probability of 0.6.

errors.label: Weighted the gain by the success probability
errors.explain: Abandonment helps in the failure state, whose probability is 0.6.

errors.label: Reported the NPV with the option
errors.explain: The option's value is the increase in NPV it creates (with minus without), not the total.

questions.explanation: The abandonment option floors the failure outcome at −$1.6M instead of −$3.8M. Its value is the probability of failure times the improvement: 0.6 × 2.2 = $1.32M. Ignoring it understates the project's NPV.

questions.stem: Northern Grain Terminals invests $4.2M today and receives $1.1M at the end of year 1. At that date (t = 1) the market turns out strong (probability 0.5), where continuing is worth $7.6M, or weak (probability 0.5), where continuing is worth $1.8M but the assets can be sold for $2.9M. These three values are measured at t = 1, not today, so discount them (with the $1.1M) once. The required return is 12%. What is the project's NPV today with the option to abandon, in $ millions?

steps.label: Weak state: best of continue 1.8 and sell 2.9
Expected value at year 1 of the best choices
Add the year-1 cash flow of 1.1
Present value today of the year-1 total

solution: Decide at the year-1 nodes first: strong, continue (7.6 > 2.9); weak, sell (2.9 > 1.8)
Expected value at the end of year 1 = 0.5 × 7.6 + 0.5 × 2.9 = 5.25
Discount one year (these amounts are at t = 1): 6.35/1.12 = 5.6696

errors.label: Continued in the weak state as well
errors.explain: The firm would sell for 2.9 rather than continue worth 1.8, so the weak state is worth 2.9.

errors.label: Forgot to discount the year-1 values
errors.explain: The 7.6, 2.9 and 1.1 are all received at t = 1, so they must be discounted one year.

errors.label: Left out the $1.1M year-1 cash flow
errors.explain: The year-1 cash flow is received whichever state follows and belongs in the PV.

questions.explanation: Take the better of continuing and selling at each year-1 node, probability-weight, add the year-1 cash flow and discount once. Here the values sit at t = 1, so unlike the pure present-value trees they must be discounted. Without abandonment NPV is $0.98M; the option adds about $0.49M.

questions.stem: Sunridge Solar has a pilot array. At the end of year 1 (t = 1), success (probability 0.35) lets it expand: the expansion costs $3.0M at t = 1 and adds cash flows worth $9.4M measured at t = 1. In failure (probability 0.65) expansion would add only $1.1M for the same cost, so the firm would not expand. These are t = 1 values, so discount them once to today. The required return is 13%. What is the option to expand worth today, in $ millions?

steps.label: Net gain from expanding in success
Expected gain at year 1 (failure: do not expand, 0)

solution: Success: expand, net gain = 9.4 − 3.0 = 6.4 (at t = 1). Failure: 1.1 < 3.0, so do not expand and gain 0

errors.label: Ignored the $3.0M cost of expanding
errors.explain: Expansion costs $3.0M, so the gain is 9.4 − 3.0, not 9.4.

errors.label: Forgot to discount the year-1 gain
errors.explain: The gain arises at the end of year 1; it must be discounted one year to give today's value.

errors.label: Forced expansion in the failure state too
errors.explain: An option is a right, not an obligation: in failure the firm simply does not expand.

questions.explanation: The option to expand is exercised only where it adds value: value = p × (added PV − cost)/(1 + R) = 0.35 × 6.4/1.13 = $1.98M. Forcing expansion in the failure state would wrongly subtract $1.9M × 0.65.

questions.stem: Cobalt Bay Mining's mill project has a static NPV of −$1.3M. Demand proves strong with probability 0.30, and then expansion adds a net present value of $6.9M (after its own cost, in today's dollars); otherwise the firm does not expand. What is the project's value including the option to expand, in $ millions?

steps.label: Expected value of the expansion option

solution: The expansion is exercised only when demand is strong: option value = 0.30 × 6.9 + 0.70 × 0 = 2.07
Total = static NPV + option value = −1.30 + 2.07 = $0.77 million (already present values, so no discounting)
The project is worth taking once its option is counted

errors.label: Ignored the option
errors.explain: The static NPV leaves out the right to expand, so it understates the project's value.

errors.label: Added the full expansion NPV
errors.explain: Expansion happens only if demand is strong, which has probability 0.30.

errors.label: Weighted by the probability of weak demand
errors.explain: The expansion value arises in the strong state, whose probability is 0.30.

questions.explanation: A negative static NPV can hide a valuable option: −1.30 + 0.30 × 6.9 = +$0.77M. The decision flips from reject to accept once the option to expand is valued.

questions.stem: Hudson Bay Marine invests $6.0M in a vessel that earns $1.5M a year for 4 years. Its resale value is $4.0M after year 1, $4.5M after year 2, $3.0M after year 3 and $1.0M after year 4 (the end of its life). Ignore taxes; the required return is 12%. What is the highest NPV across the four possible exit dates, in $ millions?

steps.label: NPV if exited at the end of year 1
NPV if exited at the end of year 2
NPV if exited at the end of year 3
NPV if exited at the end of year 4

solution: NPV(exit at year n) = −6.0 + Σ 1.5/1.12^t (t = 1..n) + resale_n/1.12^n
Exit year 1: −1.0893; year 2: 0.1224; year 3: −0.2619; year 4 (full life): −0.8085
The best exit date is the end of year 2, with NPV = $0.12 million; running the full life gives −0.81
keystrokes: Repeat with the other exit dates and compare

errors.label: Ran the vessel to the end of its life
errors.explain: Abandonment lets the firm leave when the resale value is high relative to the remaining flows; the full life is not the best date here.

errors.label: Exited after year 1
errors.explain: Exiting after year 1 gives up a good year-2 flow and resale value; compare every exit date.

errors.label: Left out the year-2 resale value
